title: Energy on the move: how it passes from thing to thing, changes form, and spreads out

summary.text: A marble rolls down a slope, knocks a cup along the table, and then everything is still. Where did the energy go? In this lesson you follow energy as it passes from one thing to another and as it changes form, in a torch, a kettle and a rolling marble. You find that it is never used up. It spreads out, mostly as warmth, and that is why things stop.
summary.art: A marble rolling down a folded card ramp towards an upturned paper cup on a table, with a torch and an electric kettle behind, and thin arrows running from one to the next.

intro.hook: Slide one coin into another coin that is lying still. The first coin stops dead, and the second one shoots away. What passed between them?
intro.text: Nothing you can see went from the first coin to the second. Yet the second coin now has the movement that the first one had. Scientists say that energy passed from one coin to the other. Now clap your hands once, hard. Your hands were moving, and then they stopped. This time the movement did not pass to another moving thing. It turned into a sound and a sting of warmth. Energy does these two things all day long: it passes along, and it changes form. Today you catch it doing both.
intro.art: Two coins on a wooden table, one sliding into the other, with a faint curved arrow jumping from the first coin to the second, and a pair of clapping hands beside them.

outcomes: I can tell an energy transfer, where energy passes from one thing to another, from an energy change, where energy changes form.
I can draw an energy chain with arrows for a torch, a kettle and a marble on a slope, from where the energy comes from to where it ends up.
I can explain that energy is never used up. It spreads out, mostly as warmth, and I can say where it went when a thing stops.
I can test fairly how the start height of a rolling marble changes how far it pushes a cup, and give my claim, my evidence and my reasoning.
I can sort the energy that comes out of a machine into the useful part and the spread-out part, and say who decides which is useful.
I can explain that in science, work means a force moving a thing, and that doing work is one way to transfer energy.
I can say what physicists mean by energy, and name one thing about it that nobody knows yet.

terms.meaning: A number that scientists can work out for anything that moves, glows, is hot, is lifted or is stretched. When things happen, the number moves from place to place, but the total stays the same.
terms.example: A marble at the top of a slope has energy because of its height.
terms.art: A marble at the top of a card ramp with a small number written beside it.

terms.meaning: Energy passing from one thing to another thing.
terms.example: A moving coin hits a still coin, and the still coin moves off with the energy.
terms.art: One coin stopped and another coin sliding away, with an arrow between them.

terms.meaning: Energy turning from one form into another form. It is also called an energy transformation or an energy conversion.
terms.example: In a torch bulb, electrical energy changes into light.
terms.art: A torch bulb with an arrow marked electrical going in and an arrow marked light coming out.

terms.meaning: One of the ways we notice energy: movement, heat, light, sound, electrical, or stored.
terms.example: A ringing bell shows energy in the form of sound.
terms.art: Six small pictures in a row: a rolling ball, a hot cup, a lamp, a bell, a plug and a stretched rubber band.

terms.meaning: The energy a thing has because it is moving. Scientists call it kinetic energy.
terms.example: A rolling marble has movement energy. The faster it rolls, the more it has.
terms.art: A marble rolling along a table with speed lines behind it.

terms.meaning: Energy that waits in a thing because of where it is, how it is shaped, or how its atoms are joined. Scientists call it potential energy.
terms.example: A marble held at the top of a slope has stored energy. So does the cell in a torch.
terms.art: A marble held still at the top of a ramp beside a torch cell.

terms.meaning: A row of words and arrows that shows where energy comes from, what it passes through, and where it ends up.
terms.example: Cell → wires → bulb → light and warmth in the room.
terms.art: Four boxes joined by arrows: a cell, a wire, a bulb and a lit room.

terms.meaning: In science, work is done when a force moves a thing. Doing work passes energy to that thing.
terms.example: When you push a swing and it moves, you do work on the swing.
terms.art: A child's hands pushing a swing seat forward, with an arrow along the push.

terms.meaning: The force between two surfaces that rub. It slows the sliding and turns movement energy into warmth.
terms.example: A paper cup sliding on a table is slowed by friction, and both get a tiny bit warmer.
terms.art: A paper cup sliding on a table with small wavy warmth lines under it.

terms.meaning: The part of the energy that does the job we wanted.
terms.example: For a bulb, the useful energy is the light.
terms.art: A bulb with a wide arrow marked light.

terms.meaning: The part of the energy that goes where we did not want it, usually as warmth or sound. Scientists say this energy is dissipated. Many books call it wasted energy.
terms.example: A mixer grinder makes noise and a warm jar. That is spread-out energy.
terms.art: A mixer grinder with small wavy lines of warmth and sound rings coming off it.

terms.meaning: The rule that energy is never made and never destroyed. It only moves and changes form.
terms.example: Add the light, the warmth and the sound from a torch, and you get exactly the energy that left the cell.
terms.art: A balance with one cell on the left pan and a small sun, a flame and a bell on the right pan, level.

terms.meaning: A drawing where the width of each arrow shows how much energy goes that way. Engineers call it a Sankey diagram.
terms.example: For a kettle, the arrow to the water is wide and the arrow to the air is narrow.
terms.art: A wide arrow splitting into one wide branch and two thin branches, drawn beside a kettle.

terms.meaning: The measure used for counting energy. Lifting a 1 litre bottle of water by 1 metre takes about 10 joules.
terms.example: A small marble rolling off a 10 centimetre slope carries about five thousandths of a joule.
terms.art: A water bottle being lifted one metre beside a ruler, with 10 J written beside it.

explanations.concept: Energy does two things: it passes along, and it changes form
explanations.definition: An energy transfer is energy passing from one thing to another. An energy change is energy turning from one form into another.
explanations.description: Watch a carrom striker hit a coin. The striker slows down and the coin speeds off. The energy was movement before, and it is movement after. Only the owner changed. That is a transfer. Now watch the coin slide to a stop on the board. Its movement did not pass to another moving thing. It turned into warmth in the board and the coin. That is a change of form. Most real events do both at once. A hot dosa on a steel plate passes heat to the plate, which is a transfer. A torch turns the stored energy of its cell into light, which is a change. When you look at anything that happens, ask two questions. Where was the energy before, and where is it now? Was it the same form before and after, or a new one?
examples: A hot cup of tea warms your hands: heat passes from the cup to your hands, and it is heat all the way.
A clap: the movement of your hands changes into sound and a little warmth.
A carrom striker hits a coin: movement passes from the striker to the coin, and a little changes into the click of the hit.

perspectives.who: Most school books, including the Cambridge and NCERT books
perspectives.explanation: Energy comes in forms, such as movement, heat, light, sound, electrical and stored. It is transferred from thing to thing and it changes from form to form.

perspectives.who: The Institute of Physics in Britain, and teachers who follow its guide
perspectives.explanation: Speaking of forms can make energy sound like a stuff that keeps changing its costume. It is clearer to say that energy sits in stores, such as a lifted thing or a hot thing, and is shifted between stores by pathways, such as a push, an electric current, heating, or light and sound.

perspectives.who: Richard Feynman, a physicist, in his lectures of 1963
perspectives.explanation: Both ways of speaking are ways of keeping accounts. Energy is a number that we can work out before and after. Nobody has seen a blob of it going from one place to another.

explanations.art: A carrom striker stopped beside a coin that is sliding away, and below it the same coin at rest with small warmth lines under it.
explanations.context: This card gives the two words of the lesson, transfer and change, and shows how to tell them apart in anything you watch.

explanations.concept: An energy chain: follow the energy
explanations.definition: An energy chain is a row of things joined by arrows. It shows where the energy came from, what it passed through, and where it ended up.
explanations.description: To draw an energy chain, start with the thing that is happening and ask where its energy came from. Then ask the same question again, and again. Write each answer in a box, and join the boxes with arrows that point the way the energy went. Above each arrow you can write how it went: by a push, by a wire, by heating, by light or by sound. A good chain also follows the energy forwards, after the job is done, until it has spread out into the room. Here is one for a pressure cooker whistle. Gas flame → hot steel → hot water → steam under pressure → the weight lifts and the steam rushes out → sound and warm, damp air in the kitchen. Almost every chain, followed far enough back, reaches the Sun. Almost every chain, followed far enough forward, ends in warmth spread through the air.
examples: Sun → paddy plant → rice → idli → your arm → a thrown ball → warmth in the air and the ground.
Falling water at Idukki dam in Kerala → turbine → generator → wires → the fan in a flat → moving air → warmth.
Cell → wire → bulb → light → the wall it lands on gets a tiny bit warmer.
explanations.art: A row of six boxes joined by arrows: a sun, a paddy plant, a plate of idlis, a child's arm, a ball in the air, and a patch of warm ground.
explanations.context: This card shows how to draw the path of energy as a chain of boxes and arrows, so that you can do it for anything at home.
explanations.one_view: A chain is an agreed way of drawing, and the closer look, that every link also leaks warmth sideways, is given in the cards on spread-out energy.

explanations.concept: Inside a torch: stored, then electrical, then light
explanations.definition: A torch changes the stored chemical energy of its cell into electrical energy, and then into light and a little warmth.
explanations.description: A torch cell holds stored energy in its chemicals. Nothing happens while the switch is off, because the path is broken. When you close the switch, the chemicals in the cell begin to react. The reaction pushes electric charge round the loop of metal, and the cell's stored energy becomes electrical energy. In the bulb, the electrical energy changes into light. Some always changes into warmth as well. Hold the front of a torch that has been on for five minutes and you can feel it. The light then crosses the room and lands on a wall or on your book. A little bounces into your eyes, which is how you see. The rest is taken in by whatever it lands on, and warms it by an amount too small to feel. So the whole chain is: stored chemical energy → electrical energy → light and warmth → warmth in the room.
examples: An LED torch front feels slightly warm after five minutes.
A phone torch runs the same chain from the phone's battery.
A dynamo torch that you squeeze starts the chain with the movement of your hand.

perspectives.who: The everyday picture, used in most school books
perspectives.explanation: Electrical energy flows along the wire from the cell to the bulb, like water through a pipe. This picture gives the right amounts and is good for drawing chains.

perspectives.who: John Henry Poynting, a physicist in Birmingham, in 1884
perspectives.explanation: The energy does not ride along inside the wire. The cell sets up an electric and magnetic field in the space around the wires, and the energy travels through that space into the bulb. The wires guide it. Physicists still work it out this way today.

explanations.art: A cut-away torch showing two cells, a metal strip, a switch and an LED, with arrows marked stored, electrical, light and a small wavy arrow marked warmth.
explanations.context: This card follows the energy through a torch, the first of the three everyday things in this lesson.

explanations.concept: Inside a kettle: electrical energy becomes heat
explanations.definition: An electric kettle changes electrical energy into heat in a metal coil, and the coil transfers the heat to the water.
explanations.description: At the bottom of an electric kettle is a metal heating coil. Electric current is pushed through it. The metal resists the current, and the electrical energy changes into heat. That is a change of form. The hot coil then passes its heat to the water that touches it. That is a transfer. The warmed water rises, cooler water sinks to take its place, and soon all the water is hot. Listen while this happens. The kettle rumbles, so a little energy has become sound. Hold your hand near the side, without touching. The wall is warm, so some heat is passing through to the air. At the end, steam carries energy out of the spout. In a good kettle, about four fifths of the electrical energy ends up in the water. A pot on a gas stove runs a different chain: the stored chemical energy of the gas changes into heat in the flame.
examples: An electric iron and a geyser make heat in the same way as a kettle.
A kettle switches itself off when steam warms a small metal strip that bends and opens the switch.
An hour after the tea is made, all the energy from the kettle has spread out into the kitchen air.
explanations.art: A cut-away electric kettle with a glowing coil at the bottom, rising loops in the water, small sound rings, a warm wall and steam from the spout, each with its own arrow.
explanations.context: This card follows the energy through an electric kettle, the second of the three everyday things in this lesson.
explanations.one_view: Measurements on kettles in many laboratories agree about where the energy goes, and no tradition of science gives a different account.

explanations.concept: A marble rolling down a slope: stored energy becomes movement
explanations.definition: A thing held high has stored energy. As it rolls down, the stored energy changes into movement energy.
explanations.description: Lift a marble to the top of a slope and hold it. Your arm did work to lift it, and that energy now waits as stored energy of height. Let go. The marble rolls faster and faster. At each moment it has a little less height and a little more movement. The stored energy is changing into movement energy, and the marble also spins as it rolls, which takes a share. At the bottom, nearly all the energy is movement. If the marble starts twice as high, it stores twice the energy, so it arrives with twice the movement energy. It does not arrive twice as fast, because movement energy grows faster than speed does. If the marble now hits a cup, its movement energy is transferred to the cup. A swing, a slide in the park and water rushing down from a dam all work the same way.
examples: A child at the top of a slide has stored energy, and at the bottom she has movement energy and a warm seat.
A cyclist freewheeling down the ghat road from Ooty turns height into speed, and the brakes turn the speed into warmth.
A swing changes stored energy into movement energy and back again, twice on every swing.
explanations.art: A marble shown at three places on a card ramp, with a tall bar marked stored at the top, equal bars in the middle, and a tall bar marked movement at the bottom.
explanations.context: This card explains what happens to the energy of a ball on a slope, the third everyday thing in this lesson, and the heart of the Marble and the Cup test.
explanations.one_view: The amounts have been measured since Galileo rolled balls down slopes in the early 1600s and are agreed. Where the stored energy of a lifted thing sits is still discussed, and that question belongs with stored energy.

explanations.concept: Work: a push that moves a thing transfers energy
explanations.definition: In science, work is done when a force moves a thing. The work done is the energy transferred to that thing.
explanations.description: When you push a toy car and it rolls, you have done work on the car. Energy has passed from your body to the car. When you lift a bucket, you do work on the bucket, and the energy waits in it as stored energy of height. The harder the push and the further the thing moves, the more work is done. Lifting a 1 litre bottle of water by 1 metre takes about 10 joules of work. Lifting it 2 metres takes about 20 joules. If the thing does not move, no work is done on it, however hard you push. Lean on a wall with all your strength. The wall does not move, so in the scientist's meaning you have done no work on the wall. Yet you feel tired. Your muscles have been changing the stored energy of your food into warmth the whole time.
examples: Pulling a suitcase along a railway platform is work, because a force moves the suitcase.
Holding a heavy school bag perfectly still does no work on the bag.
Drawing water from a well with a rope and bucket is work, and the lifted water stores the energy.

perspectives.who: Everyday speech in every language
perspectives.explanation: Work is anything that takes effort: homework, cooking, thinking, guarding a gate all night. By this meaning, holding a heavy bag for an hour is hard work.

perspectives.who: Physics, since Gaspard-Gustave Coriolis gave the word this meaning in France in 1829
perspectives.explanation: Work is a force moving a thing through a distance. It counts only the energy passed to the thing. Holding a bag still passes no energy to the bag, so the work is zero.

perspectives.who: Biologists who study muscle
perspectives.explanation: A muscle that holds still is not resting. Its tiny fibres keep pulling and letting go, many times a second, and each pull changes food energy into warmth. So the body spends energy even when the physicist's work is zero.

explanations.art: A child lifting a bucket on a rope beside another child leaning on a wall, with a tick and the word work beside the first and a cross beside the second.
explanations.context: This card gives the scientist's meaning of work, which is one of the main ways energy passes from one thing to another.

explanations.concept: Why things stop: friction changes movement into warmth
explanations.definition: Friction is the force between rubbing surfaces. It changes movement energy into warmth in both surfaces.
explanations.description: The cup in your test slid a little way and stopped. A ball rolled along the floor always stops. A swing left alone swings lower and lower. In each, the movement energy has not vanished. Wherever two surfaces rub, friction changes movement into warmth. Wherever a thing pushes through air, the air is stirred and warmed. Rub your palms together quickly ten times and you feel it at once. The amounts in the marble test are far too small to feel. A marble rolling off a 10 centimetre slope carries about five thousandths of a joule. That would warm a single drop of water by less than a tenth of a degree. With bigger things you can feel it. The brakes of a cycle are warm after a long hill. A drill bit is hot after it bores a hole. A spacecraft coming back into the air glows, because its huge movement energy changes into heat.
examples: Cycle brake blocks are warm after a long downhill ride.
A squash ball warms up to about 45 degrees Celsius during a game, from being squashed again and again.
A shooting star is a grain of space dust whose movement energy changes into heat and light in the air.

perspectives.who: What our eyes and hands tell us
perspectives.explanation: The movement ended and a different thing, warmth, appeared in its place. Movement and heat look like two separate forms of energy.

perspectives.who: The closer look, built by Count Rumford in 1798, James Joule in the 1840s and Ludwig Boltzmann in the 1870s
perspectives.explanation: Warmth is movement too. The atoms of the cup and the table never stop jiggling, and friction makes them jiggle faster. So the one orderly movement of the whole cup has become the scattered movement of countless atoms, in every direction.

explanations.art: A paper cup at rest on a table, with a magnified circle under it showing the fibres of the cup and the table jiggling.
explanations.context: This card answers the question the Marble and the Cup test leaves you with: where does the energy go when the cup stops?

explanations.concept: Energy can travel without any thing travelling with it
explanations.definition: Sound and light carry energy from place to place as waves. The air or the string shakes where it is. It does not travel along with the energy.
explanations.description: When you flick a line of touching coins, the last coin leaves and the middle coins hardly move. The energy went through them as a quick squash, passed from coin to coin. Sound travels the same way. A drum skin pushes the air next to it. That air pushes the next bit of air, and so on, all the way to your ear. No air travels from the drum to you. Only the shaking does. In a string phone, the shaking travels along a tight thread. Light also carries energy, and it needs nothing at all to travel through. Sunlight crosses 150 million kilometres of nearly empty space in about eight minutes, and warms your face when it arrives. So energy can be transferred in three ways you can test at home: by a push or a pull, by heating, and by waves of sound and light.
examples: A temple bell in Madurai shakes the air, and the shaking reaches you across the street.
A wave crosses a pond while a floating leaf only bobs up and down in its place.
Sunlight on a terrace in May makes the floor too hot for bare feet.
explanations.art: A drum on the left and an ear on the right, with rings of air between them, and one small dot of air shown shaking back and forth in its place.
explanations.context: This card explains how energy crosses a gap, as sound or as light, and why the String Phone and the Coin Line work.
explanations.one_view: How waves carry energy has been measured closely for sound and for light, and the older idea that light needs an unseen filling of space to travel through was given up after tests that began in 1887.

explanations.definition: Useful energy is the part that does the job we wanted. Spread-out energy is the part that goes elsewhere, mostly as warmth and sound.
explanations.description: No machine turns all the energy it is given into the form we want. A fan is meant to move air, but its motor also grows warm and hums. A mixer grinder is meant to grind, but it also roars and warms the chutney. An old bulb with a glowing wire turns only about a twentieth of its electrical energy into light. The rest becomes heat. An LED bulb turns about a third or more into light, so it gives the same light for far less electricity. You can draw this with an energy flow diagram. One wide arrow comes in. It splits into an arrow for the useful part and arrows for the rest, and each arrow is as wide as its share. Many books call the rest wasted energy. It is not destroyed. It has spread into the room as warmth, where it is very hard to collect and use again.
examples: A petrol car turns only about a quarter to a third of the fuel's energy into moving the car.
A phone charger feels warm, because some electrical energy becomes heat on the way to the battery.
A person cycling turns about a quarter of the food energy she spends into movement, and the rest into body warmth.

perspectives.who: Engineers
perspectives.explanation: The job decides. Any energy that does not do the job the machine was built for is wasted, and a better machine wastes less.

perspectives.who: Biologists
perspectives.explanation: For a living body, the warmth is not waste. A sparrow, a dog and a child all stay alive because the energy changes inside them keep them warm. The same warmth that an engineer calls waste in a motor is the very thing a body needs.

perspectives.who: A family in a hill town such as Kodaikanal or Shimla on a winter night
perspectives.explanation: When you want a warm room, every appliance is a heater. The warmth from the bulb, the television and the fridge is all useful. Useful is a word about what we want, and not about the energy.

explanations.art: An energy flow diagram for an old bulb and an LED bulb side by side, the first with a thin light arrow and a fat heat arrow, the second with a much fatter light arrow.
explanations.context: This card sorts the energy coming out of a machine into the part we wanted and the part that spread out, and shows how to draw it.

explanations.concept: Energy is never used up: it spreads out
explanations.definition: The total amount of energy never changes. Energy only moves and changes form. This rule is called the conservation of energy.
explanations.description: People say that a cell is finished, that the petrol is used up, or that a child has run out of energy. Scientists have measured what really happens, for nearly two hundred years, in every kind of event. They have never once found energy that vanished or energy that appeared from nowhere. When a torch cell goes flat, the energy that was stored in it now exists as a very slight warmth in the room. When your marble and cup came to rest, all the energy you gave the marble was in the table, the cup and the air. So what runs out is not energy. What runs out is energy gathered in one place, in a form that can make things happen. Once it has spread out as gentle warmth, it is all still there, but it will not gather itself again. That is why we need fuel, food and sunlight every day, even though energy is never destroyed.
examples: A flat cell weighs the same as a new one, and its energy has become warmth spread through the house.
After a firecracker, the stored chemical energy is in warm air, fading sound and scattered light.
The warmth of every fan, bus and cooking fire in a city finally leaves the Earth as heat rays into space.

perspectives.who: Everyday speech
perspectives.explanation: Energy is something you have and then use up, like money or water in a tank. This matches what we feel, because the useful, gathered energy really does run down.

perspectives.who: Julius Robert Mayer in 1842, James Joule in the 1840s and Hermann von Helmholtz in 1847
perspectives.explanation: Energy is conserved. Count every form, including the warmth, and the total before and after is always the same. Every careful test since has agreed.

perspectives.who: Some cosmologists today, such as Sean Carroll and Tamara Davis
perspectives.explanation: For things on Earth the rule holds exactly. For the whole universe, where space itself is stretching, there is no agreed way even to add up the total, so some say the rule cannot be stated for the universe as a whole.

explanations.art: A torch cell on the left with a bright glow, and on the right the same room filled with a faint even glow and the cell grey, with an equals sign between them.
explanations.context: This card states the main rule of the lesson, and explains why we can run short of fuel even though energy is never destroyed.

explanations.concept: Living beings are energy changers too
explanations.definition: Every living being takes in energy in one form and changes it into other forms to stay alive.
explanations.description: A leaf takes in light and changes it into the stored chemical energy of sugar. A parrot eats a guava and changes that stored energy into wing movement, body warmth and a loud call. A firefly changes stored chemical energy into light with very little warmth, which is why people call it cold light. An electric eel changes the energy of her food into electrical energy strong enough to stun a fish. Your own body runs a long chain all day: food → stored energy in your muscles and liver → movement, warmth, the tiny electrical signals in your nerves, and your voice. The tiny living beings in idli batter change some of the stored energy of the batter into warmth as they feed and multiply. So the energy chains in this lesson do not only run through torches and kettles. They run through every living being, and through you.
examples: A mango tree in Salem changes sunlight into the sugar of mangoes.
A honeybee shivers her flight muscles to change honey into warmth for the hive.
Your voice changes the movement of your breath and vocal folds into sound.
explanations.art: A leaf, a parrot with a guava, a firefly and a child speaking, each with one arrow coming in and two or three arrows going out, labelled with forms of energy.
explanations.context: This card shows that energy transfers and changes happen inside living beings as well as machines.
explanations.one_view: These energy changes have been measured in many living beings and are not in dispute among biologists.

explanations.concept: What do physicists mean by energy?
explanations.description: Here is what we know so far. Energy is not a thing you can see, pour or hold. It is a number that can be worked out for any object or event. There is one rule for working it out from speed, another from height, another from temperature, another from light, and more. The surprise is this. When anything happens, the numbers change in each place, but when you add them all up, the total is always the same as before. Physicists say energy is the name of that total. In 1918 the mathematician Emmy Noether proved why there must be such a number. If the laws of nature are the same today as they were yesterday, then something must stay constant, and that something is energy. What is still missing is an answer to the plain question: what is energy, underneath the sums? Nobody knows. Different people answer in different ways.
examples: You can work out the energy of a rolling marble from its mass and its speed.
You can work out the energy of a lifted marble from its mass and its height.
Add up every form before and after the marble hits the cup, and the two totals match.

perspectives.who: Richard Feynman, in The Feynman Lectures on Physics, 1963
perspectives.explanation: Energy is a number that does not change when something happens. It is a strange fact about nature and a rule for keeping accounts. Physics today has no knowledge of what energy is.

perspectives.who: Emmy Noether, a mathematician in Göttingen, in 1918
perspectives.explanation: Energy is what stays the same because the laws of nature do not change from one moment to the next. Its conservation is a mirror of that sameness in time.

perspectives.who: Friedrich Herrmann and the Karlsruhe Physics Course
perspectives.explanation: Energy can be thought of as a real quantity that flows from place to place, always carried by something, such as an electric current, moving parts, or light. Thinking of it as flowing makes its paths easy to follow.

perspectives.who: The Shakta and Kashmir Shaiva traditions of India
perspectives.explanation: Everything that happens is the play of one power, called shakti, which shows itself in every form and is never separate from awareness. This is a teaching about what the world is, and it is not a measurement.

explanations.art: A child's slate with a column of sums for speed, height, warmth and sound, a line drawn under them, and the same total written twice with a question mark beside it.
explanations.context: This card says honestly what scientists mean by the word energy, and what they still do not know about it.

agreed.text: A blunt borer turning in metal can bring cold water to the boil, again and again.
agreed.evidence: In 1798, in Munich, Count Rumford had a blunt borer turned inside a brass cannon barrel standing in water. In about two and a half hours the water boiled, and it could be done again and again. The heat came from the turning.

agreed.text: When energy seems to be missing, it has always turned up somewhere unexpected.
agreed.evidence: Around 1930, atoms that gave out an electron seemed to lose some energy without trace. Wolfgang Pauli guessed that an unseen particle was carrying it away. Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines caught that particle, the neutrino, in 1956.

agreed.text: A braking train can hand its movement back to the overhead line instead of losing it in hot brakes.
agreed.evidence: Delhi Metro trains run their motors backwards as generators when they slow down. Meters on the line show electricity flowing back for other trains to draw on.

agreed.text: Old-style lamps are better heaters than lights.
agreed.evidence: Light meters and heat meters placed around such bulbs show that nearly all the energy leaves as heat rays and warm air. This is why India's UJALA scheme, begun in 2015, replaced them with LED bulbs.

agreed.text: A ball that bounces gets warmer.
agreed.evidence: Heat cameras show a squash ball warming to about 45 degrees Celsius in play. Each bounce changes a share of the movement energy into warmth inside the rubber, which is why each bounce is lower.

agreed.text: Every claimed self-running engine has failed when tested.
agreed.evidence: Patent offices and science academies have tested claims for centuries. The Royal Academy of Sciences in Paris stopped examining such machines in 1775, because not one had worked.

challenging.claim: When a moving thing stops, its energy is gone.
challenging.for: The ball is still. The cell is flat. Nothing more happens, and nothing can be seen to have taken the energy.
challenging.against: Each time the warmth and sound have been measured, they add up to exactly the energy that seemed lost. The energy is all still there, spread too thinly to notice.
challenging.context: This is the idea most of us start with, and it is here because the whole lesson tests it.

challenging.claim: Energy does not really change form. It only moves from one store to another.
challenging.who: The Institute of Physics in Britain, following the science educator Robin Millar and others, since about 2005.
challenging.for: Talk of forms can lead children to think of energy as a stuff that turns into light, then into heat. Stores and pathways keep attention on where the energy is and how much.
challenging.against: Forms are used by most books in the world, including in India, and by many working scientists. Critics say that stores and pathways are only new labels for the same sums, and that light and sound do not fit well as either.
challenging.context: Teachers and physicists still argue about the best words for what you saw today. This card gives both sides.

challenging.claim: Energy is a real quantity that flows, like a kind of stuff.
challenging.who: Friedrich Herrmann and the Karlsruhe Physics Course in Germany, since the 1980s.
challenging.for: Energy is conserved, and you can say how much crosses any surface each second, exactly as you can for water. Treating it as flowing helps people follow it.
challenging.against: Feynman and many others answer that energy is only a number in the accounts. You cannot tag a bit of energy and follow that same bit, and how much there is depends on who is measuring.
challenging.context: Is energy a thing or a number? Physicists do not agree, and this card sets out the two answers.

challenging.claim: In the whole universe, energy is not conserved, because space is stretching.
challenging.who: Some cosmologists, such as Sean Carroll.
challenging.for: Light from far galaxies is stretched as space grows, and each bit of light loses energy with nothing nearby gaining it. The energy of empty space seems to grow as space grows.
challenging.against: Other physicists say the missing energy can be counted as energy of gravity, and that the total may even be exactly zero, as Edward Tryon proposed in 1973. Einstein's theory gives no single agreed way to add it up.
challenging.context: The rule of this lesson holds for everything on Earth. This card asks if it holds for the universe as a whole, which is still open.

challenging.claim: Energy is conserved only on average, and not in each single event between atoms.
challenging.who: Niels Bohr, Hendrik Kramers and John Slater, in 1924.
challenging.for: The first results on light and atoms were so strange that giving up exact conservation looked like a way out.
challenging.against: In 1925 Walther Bothe and Hans Geiger in Berlin, and Arthur Compton and Alfred Simon in Chicago, watched single collisions of light with electrons. Energy balanced in each one. Bohr gave the idea up.
challenging.context: Even great physicists once doubted the rule. This card tells how a test settled it.

challenging.claim: A wheel can be built that turns for ever with nothing put in.
challenging.who: Bhaskara II in India about 1150, Villard de Honnecourt in France about 1235, and hundreds of inventors since.
challenging.for: A wheel that is heavier on one side should always be falling, and a falling wheel turns.
challenging.against: Every such wheel that was built slowed and stopped. Friction changes its movement into warmth, and nothing puts that energy back. The heavy side is also balanced by more weights on the light side.
challenging.context: People in many countries have hoped for a machine that feeds itself. This card says why none has worked.

big_questions.q: If energy is never used up, why do we need to eat again tomorrow?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the energy of yesterday's food is now, and what state it is in.

big_questions.q: When a coin hits another coin, is the energy in the second coin the same energy, or new energy of the same amount?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether you could ever mark a bit of energy and follow it.

big_questions.q: Warmth is the movement of atoms. So is there really more than one form of energy?
big_questions.hint: Compare a cup sliding one way with its atoms jiggling every way.

big_questions.q: Who decides which energy is useful and which is wasted?
big_questions.hint: Think of the warm motor of a fan in May, and then on a cold night in Ooty.

big_questions.q: If all energy ends up as spread-out warmth, what will the world be like a very long time from now?
big_questions.hint: Think about what makes anything happen: a hot thing near a cold thing, a high thing above a low thing.

big_questions.q: The energy that moves your hand came from food, and before that from the Sun. Is it your energy?
big_questions.hint: Think about when it started being yours, and when it will stop.

big_questions.q: Energy is only a number we work out. Can a number be real?
big_questions.hint: Think of other things you cannot see or hold but still count, such as time or a promise.

big_questions.q: Why can spilled warmth never gather itself up again, when no rule of energy forbids it?
big_questions.hint: Try to unmix a spoon of sugar stirred into a glass of water. What would it take?

story.title: The Wheel That Kept Slowing Down
story.note: A made-up story. Manamadurai, near Madurai in Tamil Nadu, is a real town known for its clay pots and for the ghatam, a clay pot played as a drum. Many potters there still spin a heavy wheel with a stick. Valli, Kabilan and Fathima are imagined.
text: Kabilan was nine, and he had come from Chennai to Manamadurai for the Pongal holidays. Manamadurai is a town near Madurai that is known for its clay pots. His aunt Valli made pots there, as her mother had done before her.

On the first morning he sat on an upturned basket in her shed and watched. Valli Athai set the end of a long stick into a notch on her heavy wheel. She pushed the wheel round with the stick, faster and faster, nine or ten times. Then she laid the stick down. The wheel went on spinning by itself.
"You are not pushing it now," said Kabilan. "Why is it still turning?"
"I gave it my push," she said, wetting her hands. "The wheel is holding it for me."

She pressed her thumbs into a lump of grey clay in the middle of the wheel. A wall of clay rose between her fingers like something growing. But Kabilan was watching the wheel. With every press of her hands, it turned a little slower. Before the pot was done, she had to pick up the stick and spin the wheel again.
"It keeps running out," he said. "Where does the spinning go?"
"Where do you think it goes?"
"Nowhere. It just gets finished. Like my phone battery."
Valli Athai did not say he was wrong. She spun the wheel up again and lifted the pot off. "Come here. Lay your palm flat on the wooden rim while it turns. Press gently."
He pressed. The rim slid under his hand, and the wheel slowed at once, as if he had pulled a brake. In a few turns it stopped.
"Now put that palm on your cheek," she said. "Then the other one."
The palm that had touched the wheel was warm. It was not hot, but it was clearly warmer than his other hand.

"There is some of the spinning," she said. "It went into your hand. When I work, it goes into my hands and the clay. Some goes into the peg that the wheel sits on. Put your ear near the peg next time. You will hear a low hum, and the hum is some of it too. Some goes into the air that the wheel stirs."
Kabilan looked at his palm. "So it did not finish. It got out."
"It moved on," said Valli Athai. "It always moves on. Nothing in this shed keeps it for long. Not the wheel, and not me."
He thought about that. "Then where did you get it from?"

"From four idlis and a cup of sambar. And the rice and the dal got it from the Sun." She pointed with her chin at the yard, where forty wet pots stood drying. "The same Sun is working on those right now."

In the evening a girl called Fathima came from the next lane. She was eleven, and she had come to try a new ghatam. A ghatam is a clay pot that is played as a drum. Fathima sat cross-legged, set the pot against her stomach, and began to play. Her fingers, her wrists and the heels of her hands flew over the clay. The shed filled with sound, sharp at the neck of the pot and deep at its belly.
"Hold the side," she told Kabilan, without stopping. He laid two fingers on the pot. The clay was trembling.
Then she lifted her hands, and the sound died away.
"And now?" said Kabilan. "Where did the sound go?"
"You tell me, city boy," said Fathima. "You are the one with the warm hand."
He thought of the wheel. "Your hands shook the pot. The pot shook the air. The shaking went out through the door and got smaller and smaller." He stopped. "Does it turn into warmth as well?"

"That is what my science teacher says," said Fathima. "When the shaking of the air has spread out so far that nobody can hear it, it is warmth. This whole lane is warmer because I played. It is warmer by so little that no thermometer in Manamadurai could show it."
Kabilan turned to his aunt. "Then let us get it back. We can collect the warmth from the air and use it to spin the wheel. You would never need the stick."

Valli Athai smiled, but she did not laugh. "People have tried to build such a wheel for eight hundred years," she said. "Not one has worked. The warmth is all still here. But it is spread thin, like one spoon of salt stirred into the whole temple tank. I can spin this wheel with four idlis. I cannot spin it with the warm air of the shed."
"Why not? It is the same amount."
"It is the same amount," she agreed. "Keep asking why. The people who study this are still asking why the world runs only one way."

That night Kabilan lay on a mat near the shed. The wheel stood still in the dark. He counted on his fingers. Sun, rice, idli, his aunt's arm, the stick, the wheel, the pot, his warm palm. Then he thought of Fathima's playing, which was now a warmth too small to feel, somewhere in the air around him. He wondered where it would go next.
story.epiphany: When the wheel slowed, its energy was not finished. It had passed into warmth in the hand, the peg and the air, and into sound. Energy moves on and spreads out. It does not disappear, but once it is spread thin it cannot easily be gathered again.
ask: A spinning wheel slows down by itself. Name three places its energy could have gone.
Why can a potter spin a wheel with the energy of four idlis, but not with the same amount of energy spread through warm air?
Does anything keep its energy for ever? What would you look for to find out?
