A boy pressing his palm on the wooden rim of a turning potter's wheel, and then holding the same palm to his cheek with a surprised face.
A girl of eleven sitting cross-legged playing a clay ghatam, her hands a blur, with a boy resting two fingers on the side of the pot.
A boy lying on a mat at night beside a still potter's wheel, counting on his fingers, with rows of clay pots in the moonlit yard.

games.title: The Warmth Bowl: a board game where no energy is ever lost
games.players: 2 to 4 players. A parent and a child are enough.
games.context: This is a board game about the main rule of the lesson. Beans stand for energy. They pass between players and into a bowl of spread-out warmth, but the total number of beans in the game never changes.

setup.art: A hand-drawn path of twenty numbered squares snaking across a sheet of paper, with a small bowl in the middle and a pile of ten beans beside a drawn sun.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the path of 20 squares. Put a bowl in the middle and 10 beans on the Sun.

setup.art: Two players each with a small pile of twelve beans and a button on the first square, and a dice between them.
setup.caption: 2. Each player takes 12 beans and a counter. Count all the beans in the game.

setup.art: A player dropping two beans into the bowl while another reads from the board.
setup.caption: 3. Roll, move, read the square, tell the energy story, and do what it says.

printables.title: 20 squares for the path, to copy one to a square
items: 1. Start. Breakfast: three idlis gave you stored energy. Nothing to pay.
2. A ball rolls down a slope. Stored energy becomes movement. Pay 1 bean for the rubbing on the ground.
3. Carrom shot. Your striker hits a coin and stops. Pass 2 beans to the player on your left.
4. Light a room for the evening. Choose: an LED bulb, pay 1. A bulb with a glowing wire, pay 3.
5. Sunshine falls on a banana leaf. Take 2 beans from the Sun pile.
6. An electric kettle boils water for tea. Pay 1 bean for the warm air and the rumble.
7. Brakes! Your cycle stops at a signal. All its movement becomes warmth in the brake blocks. Pay 3.
8. A swing in the park. Stored energy and movement swap back and forth. Pay 1 for the air you push.
9. Pass the parcel. Give 1 bean to every other player.
10. Go 2 kilometres to school. Choose: walk or cycle, pay 1. Go by car, pay 3.
11. A solar panel on a roof in Pavagada. Take 2 beans from the Sun pile.
12. Cook the rice. Choose: a pressure cooker with its lid, pay 1. An open pot, pay 2.
13. The school bell rings. Movement becomes sound, and the sound fades into warmth. Pay 1.
14. You push a friend on a swing. Your work passes energy to her. Pass 2 beans to the player on your right.
15. The mixer grinder makes coconut chutney. Pay 2 for the roar and the warm jar.
16. A long nap. Even asleep, your body gives out warmth. Pay 1.
17. Wind turns the blades at Muppandal. The wind got its energy from the Sun. Take 1 bean from the Sun pile.
18. A phone on charge. The charger grows warm. Pay 1.
19. A mango tree feeds a parrot. Pass 1 bean to the player who has the fewest.
20. Finish. Night falls. Everyone counts every bean.

printables.title: Things to gather before you play
items: 12 beans for each player, such as rajma or chana. Each bean is one packet of energy.
10 more beans for the Sun pile.
A small bowl. This is the warmth bowl.
A button or coin for each player to move along the path.
A dice, or six paper chits numbered 1 to 6 in a cup.

printables.title: Bean count and story points
items: Player
Story points
Beans in hand at the end
Total score
All beans at the start
All beans at the end: hands, bowl and Sun pile

rules: Draw a path of 20 squares on a large sheet and copy one line of the board list into each square. Put the bowl in the middle and 10 beans on a drawn Sun.
Each player takes 12 beans. Count every bean in the game, in all hands and on the Sun, and write the total on the score sheet.
On your turn, roll the dice and move that many squares. Read your square aloud.
First tell the energy story of the square in your own words: where the energy starts and what it becomes. If the other players agree that it is right, you win 1 story point.

Then do what the square says. 'Pay' means put beans in the warmth bowl. 'Pass' means give beans to another player. 'Take' means take beans from the Sun pile. If the Sun pile is empty, you take nothing.
If you do not have enough beans, give what you have. A player with no beans keeps playing and may be passed beans later.
No bean ever comes out of the warmth bowl.
The game ends when one player reaches or passes square 20. Everyone counts the beans in all hands, in the bowl and on the Sun, and checks the total against the start.
Your score is your beans in hand plus your story points. The highest score wins. With two players, 'the player on your left' and 'on your right' are both the other player.

flow.do: Draw the path of 20 squares and copy the board lines into them. Share out 12 beans each and put 10 on the Sun. Count every bean and write the total.
flow.say: Each bean is a packet of energy. Let us count all the beans in the game before we begin. Write that number down. We will count again at the end.
flow.kid: Draw the 20 squares. Take 12 beans. Count all the beans in the game.
flow.parent: With two players the total is 34 beans. With three it is 46, and with four it is 58. You need paper, a pencil, beans, a small bowl and a dice.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Warmth Bowl. You set up and count the beans.

flow.do: Play the first few rounds. On each turn the player reads the square, tells its energy story, and then pays, passes or takes beans.
flow.say: Read your square. Before you move any beans, tell me the story. Where does the energy start? What does it become?
flow.kid: Roll and move. Read the square. Tell its energy story. Then move the beans.

ask.q: What do the beans in the bowl stand for?
good: Energy we cannot easily use again.

flow.parent: Let your child tell the story before you help. On the three choice squares, ask why one choice costs fewer beans. It is because less of the energy spreads out as warmth.
flow.context: In this step, you play the first rounds and tell the energy story of each square.

flow.do: Play on until one player reaches or passes square 20.
flow.say: Keep going. Watch the bowl. Is it filling or emptying? Has anything come back out of it?
flow.kid: Play to square 20. Watch the bowl fill up.
flow.parent: A game usually takes six or seven turns each. Nobody can get stuck, because a player with no beans still moves.
flow.context: In this step, you finish the game and watch the warmth bowl fill.

flow.do: Count the beans in every hand, in the bowl and on the Sun. Add them and compare with the starting total. Then add up the scores.
flow.say: Let us count every bean. Hands, bowl and Sun. Is it the same number we started with? Where are most of the beans now?
flow.kid: Count all the beans again. Is the total the same? Where are most of them?
flow.parent: The total always matches, unless a bean rolled off the table. That is the rule of conservation. Most beans end in the bowl, as spread-out warmth.
flow.think: Why does the game have no square that says 'take beans from the warmth bowl'? Would such a square be true to the real world?
flow.context: In this step, you check that the total number of beans never changed, and find the winner.

experiments.title: The Marble and the Cup: does twice the height give twice the push?
experiments.question: If a marble starts twice as high on a slope, does it push a paper cup twice as far?
experiments.predict: Before you roll anything, guess. From the 20 mark, will the cup slide the same distance as from the 10 mark, a bit further, twice as far, or more than twice as far? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Only the starting mark of the marble changes: 10, 20 and 30 centimetres up the ramp. The ramp, the marble, the cup, the table and the cup's starting place stay the same. The marble is let go and never pushed. Each mark is tried three times, because one roll can go crooked, and the middle distance of the three is used.
results_table: Height of the mark above the table

materials.item: a glass marble, with one spare in case it rolls away
a strip of stiff card 30 centimetres long and 8 centimetres wide, cut from a cereal box and folded along its length into a V
a pile of books about 10 centimetres high
a paper cup (or an empty toothpaste box cut to the length of a finger, open at one end)
a ruler, sticky tape and a pencil
scissors, for the grown-up
a smooth table or floor with 60 centimetres of clear space
the results table on paper

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the card and the doorway in the cup. Keep marbles away from children under five, and pick them up from the floor when you finish.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw three bars for the three middle slides, side by side, and write one sentence each for your claim, your evidence and your reasoning.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you let a marble roll down a ramp into a paper cup and measure how far the cup is pushed. You find out how the push depends on the height the marble starts from, and then you ask where the energy went.

setup.art: A strip of cereal-box card folded into a long V, with pencil marks at 10, 20 and 30 centimetres from one end.
setup.caption: 1. Fold the card into a V. Mark 10, 20 and 30 centimetres from the bottom end.

setup.art: The V ramp with its top end resting on a pile of books and its bottom end taped to a table.
setup.caption: 2. Rest the top on 10 centimetres of books. Tape the bottom to the table.

setup.art: An upturned paper cup with a small square doorway cut in its rim, facing the bottom of the ramp, with a pencil outline drawn round the cup.
setup.caption: 3. Cut a doorway in the cup. Stand the cup upside down at the end of the ramp and draw round it.

setup.art: A hand letting go of a marble at the 20 mark, and the cup further along the table with a ruler measuring from the pencil outline.
setup.caption: 4. Let the marble go from a mark. Measure how far the cup slid from its outline.

setup.art: A table of results with three rows and a small bar chart of three bars beside it.
setup.caption: 5. Try each mark three times. Write the middle slide and draw the bars.

flow.do: Show your child the folded card, the marble and the cup. Explain that the marble will roll into the cup from three heights. Write down their guess and their reason.
flow.say: The marble will roll down and push the cup. From the 20 mark it starts twice as high as from the 10 mark. How far will the cup slide then? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The marble will push the cup. Guess how far from each mark. Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think it will slide that far?
good: Because it has more energy at the top.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Common guesses are 'the same', 'a bit more' and 'much more, because it is faster'. All are worth testing. Write the guess and the reason above the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Marble and the Cup. You guess before you roll.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts the card strip and a doorway in the cup rim, about 3 centimetres wide and 3 centimetres high. Fold the card into a V. Mark 10, 20 and 30 centimetres from the bottom end. Rest the top on the books and tape the bottom to the table. Stand the cup upside down with its doorway touching the end of the ramp. Draw round the cup.
flow.say: Let us build it. I will do the cutting. You make the marks at 10, 20 and 30. Now measure how high each mark is above the table.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts. You mark 10, 20 and 30 on the ramp. Draw round the cup.
flow.parent: With the top end 10 centimetres high, the three marks are about 3, 7 and 10 centimetres above the table. Let your child measure them with the ruler held upright, and write them in the table. The 20 mark is twice as high as the 10 mark, and the 30 mark is three times as high. Roll the marble once to check that it enters the doorway. If it misses, straighten the ramp and tape it again.

check.q: The ramp is straight. The 10 mark is 3 centimetres above the table. About how high is the 30 mark?
check.why: On a straight ramp, three times as far along is three times as high, so about 9 or 10 centimetres. If you picked 30, you gave the distance along the ramp and not the height above the table.

flow.context: In this step, you build the ramp and mark the three starting places.

flow.do: Hold the marble on the 10 mark and let go without pushing. Measure from the pencil outline to the nearest edge of the cup. Put the cup back on its outline. Do this three times. Then do three rolls from the 20 mark and three from the 30 mark.
flow.say: Put the marble on the mark. Just open your fingers. Do not push. Now measure how far the cup slid from its outline, and write it down.
flow.kid: Let the marble go. Do not push. Measure the slide. Put the cup back each time.

ask.q: What did you hear when the marble hit the cup?
good: It was louder from the top mark.

flow.parent: From the lowest mark the cup may slide 3 to 6 centimetres, and from the top mark 10 to 18. Yours will depend on your cup and table, so write what you see. If the cup falls over, lower the book pile to 6 centimetres and start again. If the cup hardly moves, try a smoother surface or a lighter cup. If the marble bounces out without pushing, turn the doorway squarely to the ramp. Do not count a roll where the marble missed the door. With two or more children, one lets go, one measures and one writes, and they swap after each mark.
flow.context: In this step, you roll the marble three times from each mark and measure each slide.

flow.do: For each mark, find the middle of the three slides. Write it in the last column. Draw three bars, one for each middle slide, using one square of the page for each centimetre.
flow.say: Look at your three numbers for the 10 mark. Which one is in the middle? That is the one we keep. Now draw a bar for each mark.
flow.kid: Find the middle number for each mark. Draw three bars.

ask.q: The 20 mark is twice as high as the 10 mark. Is its bar about twice as tall?

flow.parent: The middle value is used because one odd roll then changes nothing. Now compare. Many families find the 20 mark gives roughly twice the slide of the 10 mark, and the 30 mark roughly three times. It will not be exact. If your bars show something else, that is your real result, so keep it and talk about what might have caused it.

check.q: From the 10 mark the slides were 4, 6 and 5 centimetres. Which number do you keep?
check.why: Put them in order: 4, 5, 6. The middle one is 5. If you picked 6, you chose the biggest. The middle value is fairer, because one lucky roll does not change it.

flow.context: In this step, you find the middle slide for each mark and draw the results as bars.

flow.do: Ask your child to write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why. Then ask where the marble's energy is now that the cup has stopped. Rub a palm hard on the table ten times and feel the palm.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you now think happens when the marble starts higher? What did you see? Why do you think it happens? Then tell me this. The cup has stopped. Where is the energy now?
flow.kid: Write what you think, what you saw, and why. The cup stopped. Where did its energy go?
flow.parent: Only after your child has answered, give the idea. A higher start stores more energy. Rolling down changes it into movement. The hit transfers it to the cup. Friction with the table then changes it into warmth, and each centimetre of sliding takes about the same amount. So twice the energy lasts about twice as far. The click was a little of the energy leaving as sound. Say plainly what the test cannot show: you did not measure the warmth. It is far too small to feel, about five thousandths of a joule. The palm rub lets you feel the same change with a bigger amount. Ask what else your child would test, such as a heavier marble or a rougher table.
flow.think: You gave the marble its height with your arm. Where did your arm get that energy, and where is that energy now?
flow.context: In this step, you say what the results show, and then you ask where the energy went when the cup stopped.

experiments.title: The Tired Swing: does a sail make a pendulum run down sooner?
experiments.question: A swinging bunch of keys slowly swings less and less. If it has to push more air, does it run down sooner, and by how much?
experiments.predict: Guess how many swings the keys will make before the swing is half as wide. Then guess the number when a postcard is opened out on the keys like a sail. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Only the card changes: folded small for the first three runs, and opened flat to face the air for the next three. The thread, the keys, the card itself and the starting mark stay the same. The card rides on the keys in both tests, so the weight is the same. Each test is done three times and the middle count is used.

materials.item: cotton thread about 80 centimetres long
a bunch of three keys on a ring
an old postcard or a piece of thin card about 10 by 15 centimetres
sticky tape
a strip of paper 50 centimetres long, a ruler and a pencil
a table, and the results table on paper

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Write how many times sooner the swing ran down with the sail open, and one sentence on where the energy went.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you make a pendulum from keys and thread and count its swings as it runs down. You test whether pushing more air makes it lose its energy sooner.

setup.art: A bunch of keys hanging on a thread taped to the edge of a table, just clear of the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Tape the thread to the table edge. The keys hang just above the floor.

setup.art: A paper strip on the floor under the keys with marks at 0, 10 and 20 centimetres.
setup.caption: 2. Lay the strip under the keys. Mark 0 under them, then 10 and 20 to one side.

setup.art: A postcard folded small and taped to the bunch of keys, and beside it the same postcard opened flat and taped so that it faces the direction of the swing.
setup.caption: 3. Tape the card on the keys. First folded small, later opened flat.

setup.art: A child looking down from above as the keys swing over the paper strip, counting on her fingers.
setup.caption: 4. Let go at 20. Count swings until the keys stop reaching 10.

flow.do: Hang the keys and swing them once so that your child sees the swing slowly getting smaller. Stop them. Ask for both guesses and the reasons, and write them down.
flow.say: The swing gets smaller by itself. How many swings before it is half as wide? What if the keys carry an open card? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess the swings with the card folded. Guess again with the card open. Say why.
flow.parent: One swing means there and back. Do not correct the guess. Many children expect only a small difference.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Tired Swing. You guess before you count.

flow.do: Tape one end of the thread firmly to the top of the table at its edge. Tie the keys to the other end so that they hang 2 centimetres above the floor. Lay the paper strip on the floor under the swing. Mark 0 under the still keys, and 10 and 20 centimetres to one side. Fold the card three times and tape it flat against the keys.
flow.say: Let us hang the keys so that they just clear the floor. Now mark the strip. Zero is under the keys. Then mark 10 and 20.
flow.kid: Hang the keys low. Mark 0, 10 and 20 on the strip. Tape on the folded card.
flow.parent: Press two or three pieces of tape over the thread so that it cannot slip. The keys must swing along the strip, not across it. Looking straight down from above gives the best view of the marks.
flow.context: In this step, you build the pendulum and mark where the swing starts and where it is half as wide.

flow.do: Pull the keys to the 20 mark with the thread tight. Let go without pushing. Count each time the keys come back to your side. Stop counting when they no longer reach the 10 mark. Write the count. Do it three times.
flow.say: Hold the keys over the 20 mark. Let go. Count each time they come back to you. Stop when they do not reach the 10 mark any more.
flow.kid: Let go at 20. Count each return. Stop when they miss the 10 mark.

ask.q: Did the keys ever swing back further than the 20 mark where you let go?
good: They came back a little short each time.

flow.parent: Expect somewhere between 20 and 80 swings. Each run takes one to two minutes. Count aloud together. If the keys wobble in a circle, stop and start that run again.
flow.context: In this step, you count the swings with the card folded small.

flow.do: Unfold the card. Tape it to the keys so that its flat face meets the air as the keys swing. Start from the 20 mark again and count in the same way, three times.
flow.say: Now the card is open like a sail. Same start, same counting. Let go.
flow.kid: Open the card. Tape it to face the air. Count the swings again.
flow.parent: Expect only about 3 to 10 swings. If the card twists edge-on, add a second piece of tape so that it stays facing the swing.
flow.context: In this step, you count the swings with the card opened out to push the air.

flow.do: Find the middle count for each test. Divide the bigger by the smaller to see how many times sooner the sail swing ran down. Ask your child to write what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think the air does to a swing? What did you count? Why did the open card make such a difference?
flow.kid: Write what you think, what you saw and why. Where did the swing's energy go?
flow.parent: After your child has answered, give the idea. At each end of the swing, the keys have stored energy of height. In the middle it is movement energy. It changes back and forth, twice on every swing. Each time, the keys and card push air aside, and some movement becomes warmth in the air. The open card pushes far more air, so the energy leaves far sooner. A little also leaves where the thread bends under the tape. What the test cannot tell you is how the loss is shared between the air and the thread. Ask how your child would find out.

check.q: With the card folded the middle count was 40 swings. With it open, 5. How many times sooner did the open card run down?
check.why: 40 divided by 5 is 8, so the swing ran down 8 times sooner. If you picked 35, you subtracted. 'How many times' asks you to divide.

flow.think: A swing in the park also runs down. What would you change to make it keep going longer?
flow.context: In this step, you compare the two counts and say where the energy of the swing went.

activities.title: Pass It or Change It? Five quick tests on a table

materials.item: coins of the same kind
a torch, or the torch of a phone
a ball of atta dough the size of a lemon, on a clean steel plate
a smooth table

schedule.what: Do five quick tests: a coin hit, a clap, a palm rub, a torch and a dropped ball of dough. Sort them into passed along and changed form.

activities.record: Draw two columns headed 'passed along' and 'changed form'. Write each of the five tests where you think it belongs. Some may go in both.
activities.context: In this activity, you do five tiny tests and ask the same two questions each time. Where was the energy before, and where is it after? You meet the two main words of the lesson, transfer and change.

setup.art: Two coins on a table, one being slid by a finger towards the other.
setup.caption: 1. Slide one coin into a still coin. Watch both.

setup.art: A child clapping, and then rubbing her palms together.
setup.caption: 2. Clap once. Then rub your palms ten times.

setup.art: A torch shining on a wall beside a ball of dough flattened on a steel plate.
setup.caption: 3. Switch on a torch. Drop a ball of dough on a plate.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with two columns, passed along and changed form, and five small drawings placed in them.
setup.caption: 4. Sort the five tests into two columns.

flow.do: Put one coin on the table. Slide the other coin into it, straight on. Watch what each coin does. Do it three times.
flow.say: Slide this coin into that one. What does the first coin do? What does the second one do? What do you think passed between them?
flow.kid: Slide one coin into the other. Watch both coins. What passed between them?

ask.q: The first coin stopped. Where did its movement go?
good: It gave it to the second coin.

flow.parent: With a straight hit, the first coin nearly stops and the second moves off. Do not give the word energy yet. Let your child find words for it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Pass It or Change It. You watch movement go from one coin to another.

flow.do: Clap your hands once, hard. Then rub your palms together quickly ten times and hold them to your cheeks.
flow.say: Clap once. Your hands were moving and then they stopped. What did the movement turn into? Now rub your palms ten times. What do you feel?
flow.kid: Clap once. Rub your palms ten times. What did the movement turn into?

ask.q: In the clap, did the movement pass to another moving thing, or turn into something else?
good: It turned into a sting and warmth.

flow.context: In this step, you turn the movement of your hands into sound and into warmth.

flow.do: Switch on the torch and shine it on a wall. Then hold the ball of dough 30 centimetres above the plate and let go. Look at its shape and listen.
flow.say: Where is the torch getting its light from? Now drop the dough. What happened to its shape? What did you hear?
flow.kid: Shine the torch. Then drop the dough on the plate. Look and listen.
flow.parent: The dough does not bounce. Its movement went into squashing it, a thud, and a very small warmth. Keep the dough on the clean plate so that it can be used for a chapati afterwards.
flow.context: In this step, you watch stored energy change into light, and then into a thud and a flat shape.

flow.do: Give the two words. A transfer is energy passing from one thing to another. A change is energy turning into a new form. Ask your child to place each of the five tests in a column.
flow.say: Scientists call what passed between the coins energy. When it passes along, that is a transfer. When it turns into a new form, that is a change. Where does each test go?
flow.kid: Passed along is a transfer. A new form is a change. Sort your five tests.
flow.parent: The coin hit is mainly a transfer. The clap, the rub, the torch and the dough are changes of form. Accept 'both' with a reason, because the coin hit also made a click.

check.q: A hot idli warms the cold plate under it. Is this mainly a transfer or a change of form?
check.why: Heat passes from the idli to the plate, and it is heat before and after, so it is a transfer. If you picked a change, ask yourself what new form appeared.

flow.think: Can you think of something that happens with no transfer and no change of energy at all?
flow.context: In this step, you learn the words transfer and change, and sort the five tests.

activities.title: Kettle Watch: draw the energy with wide and thin arrows

materials.item: an electric kettle with two cups of water in it (or a small pot of water heated by a grown-up)
paper and two colour pencils
a ruler

activities.safety: A grown-up fills, switches on and pours. Children stand an arm's length away and never put a hand over the spout, because steam burns. Use the hot water for tea or cooking afterwards.

schedule.what: Watch and listen to a kettle from cold to boiling. Draw an energy flow diagram with a wide arrow for the water and thin arrows for the rest.

activities.record: Keep the energy flow diagram, with each arrow labelled, and one sentence on where all the energy is an hour later.
activities.context: In this activity, you watch a kettle boil and notice every place the energy goes. Then you draw it as an energy flow diagram, where the width of each arrow shows the share.

setup.art: A parent switching on an electric kettle while a child stands back with paper and pencils.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up switches on the kettle. Stand an arm's length away.

setup.art: A child holding her open hand near the side of a kettle without touching, and cupping her ear.
setup.caption: 2. Listen. Feel the air near the side, without touching.

setup.art: A drawing of one wide arrow entering a kettle and splitting into one wide arrow and three thin arrows.
setup.caption: 3. Draw one wide arrow in. Split it into a wide arrow and thin arrows.

flow.do: A grown-up puts two cups of water in the kettle and switches it on. Ask your child where the energy is coming from and where it will go. Write the guesses.
flow.say: I have switched the kettle on. Where is the energy coming from? Name every place you think it will go.
flow.kid: A grown-up switches on the kettle. Where will the energy go? Name each place.
flow.parent: If you have no electric kettle, heat a small pot of water on the stove and keep your child an arm's length back. The chain then starts with the stored chemical energy of the gas.
flow.context: This is the first step of Kettle Watch. You guess where the energy will go.

flow.do: Stay with the kettle. Listen for the first hiss and the rumble. Hold a hand 10 centimetres from the side, without touching. Watch for steam and for the switch clicking off.
flow.say: What can you hear? Is the air near the side warm? What is coming out of the spout? Each of those is energy going somewhere.
flow.kid: With a grown-up, listen to the kettle. Feel the warm air near it. Do not touch.

ask.q: Which things that you noticed were not the job of the kettle?
good: The steam going into the room.

flow.context: In this step, you notice the sound, the warm wall and the steam of a boiling kettle.

flow.do: Draw what you watched. Draw one arrow coming in, 5 squares wide, and label it electrical. Split it into two parts. One arrow is 4 squares wide, labelled heats the water. Thin arrows show the warm air, the sound and the steam.
flow.say: Let us draw it. The arrow in is five squares wide. About four of the five parts heat the water. Draw that arrow four squares wide. Share the last square between the thin arrows.
flow.kid: Draw a wide arrow in. Split it. Four parts heat the water. One part goes elsewhere.
flow.parent: The widths going out must add up to the width coming in, because no energy is lost or made. This kind of drawing is called a Sankey diagram, after the engineer Matthew Sankey, who drew one for a steam engine in 1898.

check.q: The arrow going in is 5 squares wide. The arrow to the water is 4 squares wide. How wide are all the other arrows together?
check.why: What goes out must equal what comes in. 5 take away 4 leaves 1 square for everything else. If you picked 9, you added, which would mean the kettle made extra energy.

flow.context: In this step, you draw an energy flow diagram for the kettle you watched.

flow.do: Ask where all the energy will be in one hour, when the tea has been drunk and everything is cold again.
flow.say: In an hour the water will be cold again. Where will all that energy be then?
flow.kid: In one hour the water is cold. Where is the energy then?
flow.parent: A good answer is that it has spread into the kitchen air, the cups and the people who drank the tea, and is on its way out of the house.
flow.think: Is the energy in the hot water useful energy or spread-out energy when you forget the tea and it goes cold?
flow.context: In this step, you follow the energy forwards, after the kettle's job is done.

activities.title: The Coin Line: send energy through coins that stay still

materials.item: coins of the same kind, such as two-rupee coins
a ruler, to line the coins up against
a smooth table

schedule.what: Line up five touching coins. Flick one coin into the end, then two. Watch how many leave the far end.

activities.record: Draw the line of coins before and after, for one coin in and for two coins in. Mark the coins that moved.
activities.context: In this activity, you flick a coin into a line of touching coins and see the coin at the far end leave. You watch energy pass through things that hardly move.

setup.art: Five coins in a touching row along the edge of a ruler on a table, with a sixth coin a little way off.
setup.caption: 1. Line up five coins, touching, along a ruler.

setup.art: A finger flicking the sixth coin into the end of the row, and the coin at the far end sliding away.
setup.caption: 2. Flick one coin into the end. Watch the other end.

setup.art: Two coins sliding together into the row and two coins leaving the far end.
setup.caption: 3. Slide two coins in together. Count how many leave.

flow.do: Line up five coins so that each touches the next, along the edge of the ruler. Put the sixth coin 5 centimetres from one end. Ask what will happen when it is flicked into the row.
flow.say: I will flick this coin into the end of the row. What will the row do? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Line up five touching coins. Guess what happens when one coin hits the end.
flow.parent: Common guesses are that the whole row will slide, or that the coins will scatter. Write the guess down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Coin Line. You guess before you flick.

flow.do: Flick the sixth coin straight into the end of the row, along the ruler. Watch the far end. Reset the row and do it five times.
flow.say: Flick it straight in. Which coin moved? Which coins stayed?
flow.kid: Flick the coin in. Which coin leaves? Which coins stay still?

ask.q: The middle coins hardly moved. How did the energy reach the last coin?
good: Each coin passed it to the next.

flow.parent: With a straight flick, the last coin leaves and the others barely move. A crooked flick scatters them, so keep the ruler as a guide. It is not perfect. Sometimes a second coin creeps a little.
flow.context: In this step, you see one coin leave the far end while the middle coins stay.

flow.do: Now hold two coins together and slide both into the row at once. Count how many leave the far end. Try it five times.
flow.say: This time two coins go in together. How many do you think will leave?
flow.kid: Slide two coins in together. Count how many leave the other end.
flow.parent: Usually two coins leave. It is harder to do cleanly than one coin, so count the tries where the two went in together.
flow.context: In this step, you send in two coins and count how many leave.

flow.do: Talk about what passed along the row. Then give the idea: each coin was squashed a tiny bit and sprang back, pushing the next.
flow.say: The energy went through four coins that stayed where they were. It passed along as a quick squash. Sound moves through air in the same way.
flow.kid: The energy passed through the still coins as a quick squash. Sound travels like that too.
flow.think: After a few seconds the last coin stops too. Where is the energy of your flick then?
flow.context: In this step, you explain how energy got through the coins, and link it to sound.

activities.title: The String Phone: can sound energy travel along a thread?

materials.item: paper cups
cotton thread about 4 metres long
a pointed pencil, for the grown-up to make the holes
short pieces of matchstick or two paper clips
a second person to talk to

activities.safety: A grown-up makes the hole in each cup with the pencil point, pushing away from the hand.

schedule.what: Make a phone from two paper cups and a thread. Test it with the thread tight, slack and pinched.

activities.record: Draw the energy chain from the speaker's voice to the listener's ear, with an arrow for each step. Write what happened with the thread tight, slack and pinched.
activities.context: In this activity, you make a phone from two paper cups and a thread. You find out how the energy of a voice can pass along a thread, and what stops it.

setup.art: A parent pushing a pencil point through the bottom of a paper cup.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up makes a small hole in the bottom of each cup.

setup.art: A thread passing through the bottom of a cup and tied to a piece of matchstick inside.
setup.caption: 2. Thread each end through a cup. Tie it to a bit of matchstick inside.

setup.art: Two people standing across a room with the thread pulled tight between two cups, one speaking and one listening.
setup.caption: 3. Pull the thread tight. One speaks into a cup, one listens.

flow.do: A grown-up makes a small hole in the bottom of each cup. Push one end of the thread through each hole from outside. Tie each end round a piece of matchstick so that it cannot slip out.
flow.say: I will make the holes. You push the thread through and tie it to the matchstick inside the cup.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes the holes. You tie the thread inside each cup.
flow.context: This is the first step of the String Phone. You build it.

flow.do: Before testing, ask your child to guess. Will a whisper be heard with the thread tight? With the thread loose? Write the guesses and reasons.
flow.say: One of us will whisper into a cup. Will the other hear it when the thread is tight? What about when it hangs loose? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Will a whisper get through a tight thread? A loose thread? Say why.
flow.context: In this step, you guess what the thread will do before you test it.

flow.do: Stand as far apart as the thread allows and pull it tight. One person whispers into a cup while the other holds a cup to the ear. Then let the thread hang loose and try again. Then pull it tight and have someone pinch the thread in the middle.
flow.say: Hold the cup to your ear. I will whisper. Now we let it go loose. Now tight again, and I pinch the middle. What changed each time?
flow.kid: Whisper with the thread tight. Then loose. Then pinched. What changes?

ask.q: Touch the tight thread lightly while someone speaks. What do you feel?

flow.parent: The thread must be straight and must not touch furniture. The whisper comes through clearly when it is tight, and not when it is loose or pinched. If nothing comes through, check that the knots sit against the cup bottoms.
flow.context: In this step, you test the phone with the thread tight, loose and pinched.

flow.do: Draw the chain together: voice, air in the cup, cup bottom, thread, second cup bottom, air, ear. Ask what kind of energy it is at each step.
flow.say: Your voice shakes the air. The air shakes the cup. The cup shakes the thread. What form is the energy all the way along?
flow.kid: Draw the chain from mouth to ear. What form is the energy all along?
flow.parent: It is movement energy passed along as a shaking, which is what sound is. So this is nearly all transfer, with little change of form. A pinch takes the shaking into your fingers.
flow.think: A loose thread carries no whisper. What is different about a tight one?
flow.context: In this step, you draw the energy chain of the string phone.

projects.title: The Chain Diary: three days, three energy chains

materials.item: strips of paper about 30 centimetres long
a pencil and a red colour pencil
a large sheet of paper or an old calendar page, and glue or tape

schedule.what: A kitchen chain. Pick one thing that happens in your kitchen and draw its energy chain on a strip.
A journey chain. Pick one trip and draw the chain for what moved you.
A living chain. Draw the chain for a living being near you. Stick all three strips on a poster and mark in red where warmth spread out.

projects.record: Keep the poster with three chains. Each chain goes back as far as you can trace it, and forward until the energy has spread out. Red marks show every place where warmth leaked away.
projects.context: In this project, you draw one energy chain a day for three days: one from the kitchen, one from a journey and one from a living being. Then you look for what all three have in common.

setup.art: A child at a kitchen doorway drawing boxes and arrows on a paper strip while an idli steamer steams on the counter.
setup.caption: 1. Day 1: draw the chain for one thing in the kitchen.

setup.art: A child on a city bus seat looking out, with a paper strip and pencil on her lap.
setup.caption: 2. Day 2: draw the chain for one journey.

setup.art: Three paper strips stuck on a poster, each a row of boxes and arrows, with red wavy marks under several arrows.
setup.caption: 3. Day 3: add a living chain. Mark the warmth leaks in red.

flow.do: Choose one thing that happens in your kitchen today, such as idlis steaming, a mixer grinding or a fridge humming. On a strip, draw a box for it. Ask where its energy came from, and draw that box to the left, with an arrow. Keep going back. Then go forward: where does the energy go afterwards?
flow.say: Pick one thing happening here. Where does its energy come from? And where did that come from? Now go the other way. Where does the energy go when the job is done?
flow.kid: Pick one kitchen thing. Draw where its energy came from. Draw where it goes next.

good: In me, when I eat it.

flow.parent: Watch from the doorway. Nothing needs to be touched. If your child is stuck going back, say that electricity in many South Indian homes comes from coal, falling water, wind and sunlight, all mixed in the wires. Any one of them is a fair box.
flow.context: This is the first day of the Chain Diary. You draw a chain from the kitchen.

flow.do: Choose one journey from today: a walk, a cycle ride, a bus, an auto-rickshaw or a lift. Draw its chain on the second strip. Add what happens to the movement energy when the journey stops.
flow.say: What moved you today? Where did it get its energy? When it stopped at the end, where did the movement go?
flow.kid: Pick one trip. Draw what moved you. Where did the movement go at the end?
flow.parent: For a bus, the chain is diesel, engine, wheels, moving bus, and then warm brakes and air. For a walk it begins with breakfast. Either way it ends in warmth.
flow.context: This is the second day of the Chain Diary. You draw the chain for a journey.

flow.do: Choose a living being you can watch, such as a crow, a potted tulsi plant, a street dog or yourself. Draw the chain on the third strip. Then stick all three strips on the poster. With red, mark every arrow where some warmth or sound leaks away.
flow.say: Now a living chain. Where does this being get energy, and what does the energy become? Then let us mark every place on all three chains where warmth leaks out.
flow.kid: Draw a chain for a living being. Stick up all three. Mark the warmth leaks in red.
flow.parent: Almost every arrow earns a red mark. That is the finding. Ask what all three chains share at the start and at the end.
flow.think: All three chains end in spread-out warmth. Can you invent a chain that does not?
flow.context: This is the third day of the Chain Diary. You add a living chain and compare all three.

challenges.title: The Long Spin: build a top that keeps its energy longest
challenges.problem: Build a spinning top from things at home. Give it energy with one twist of your fingers. Make it spin for as long as you can before all that energy has spread out as warmth and sound. There is more than one good design.
constraints: Start the top with one twist of the fingers of one hand. No string and no motor.
The top must spin by itself on a plate or table. Nobody touches it after the twist.
Time three spins with a stopwatch. Your best time counts.
Change one thing at a time, so that you know what made the difference.
materials: stiff card from a cereal box, or an old CD
a matchstick, a toothpick or a short pencil
coins, sticky tape and a ball of atta dough or clay
a plastic bottle cap and a marble
a steel plate, and a phone stopwatch
challenges.safety: A grown-up cuts the card and pushes the stick through its centre.
general: Push the stick through the exact centre of a card disc about 8 centimetres across, so that the top does not wobble.
Keep the disc low on the stick, close to the plate, so that it does not fall over.
Tape coins evenly round the rim. A heavy rim holds more movement energy from the same twist.
creative: Rest an old CD on a marble, with a bottle cap taped on top as a handle. The marble makes a smooth round tip.
Spin the top inside a shallow steel bowl, so that it cannot wander off and hit the rim of a plate.
Compare the same top on a steel plate, a tile, a newspaper and a towel, to find which surface takes its energy fastest.
challenges.your_turn: Build your own top and time it. What did you change that helped the most? Where do you think its energy went fastest: into the tip, into the air or into wobbling?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about losing energy slowly. A spinning top holds movement energy, and friction at its tip and with the air changes that energy into warmth. You try to slow the loss.

setup.art: A card disc with a matchstick pushed through its centre, held between a finger and thumb above a steel plate.
setup.caption: 1. Make a disc with a stick through its centre.

setup.art: A top spinning on a steel plate beside a phone showing a stopwatch.
setup.caption: 2. Twist once. Time the spin until the disc touches the plate.

setup.art: Three different tops in a row: a card disc with coins taped round the rim, a CD resting on a marble, and a plain small disc.
setup.caption: 3. Change one thing. Time it again.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask your child what makes a top stop, and what might make it spin longer. Write the ideas down.
flow.say: A top always stops in the end. Where does its energy go? What could you change so that it goes more slowly?
flow.kid: Why does a top stop? Think of ways to make it spin longer.

ask.q: Where does a top's energy go?

flow.context: This is the first step of the Long Spin. You plan.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts a card disc about 8 centimetres across and pushes a matchstick through its centre. Spin it on the steel plate with one twist. Time three spins and write the best.
flow.say: I will cut the disc and make the hole. You spin it. One twist, then hands off. I will time it.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts the disc. You twist it once. Time three spins.
flow.parent: A plain card top spins for about 5 to 15 seconds. That time is the one to beat. If it wobbles, the stick is off centre, so make a new hole.
flow.context: In this step, you build a first plain top and time it.

flow.do: Change one thing and time three spins again. Try a heavier rim, a lower disc, a smoother tip or a different surface. Keep a list of each change and its best time.
flow.say: Change one thing only. What do you want to try first? Why do you think it will help?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Time it again. Write the change and the time.
flow.parent: Coins on the rim usually help most, and a CD on a marble can spin for over a minute. Let your child find this out. A change that makes it worse is also a finding.
flow.context: In this step, you test your ideas one at a time.

flow.do: Look at the list together. Ask which change helped most and why. Listen to the best top as it slows.
flow.say: Which change gave the longest spin? Why do you think it worked? In the end it still stopped. Where is the energy of your twist now?
flow.kid: Which change helped most? The top still stopped. Where is the energy now?
flow.think: Could any top spin for ever? What would have to be true?
flow.context: In this step, you say what worked and where the energy of the spin went.

videos.title: "Our World: Potential and Kinetic Energy" by Adventure Academy
videos.why: To see stored energy change into movement energy and back on a roller coaster, the same change your marble made on its ramp.
videos.check: Id confirmed with YouTube (title and channel match). Length is an estimate. A parent should preview it first.

videos.title: Potential and Kinetic Energy – Newton's Cradle
videos.why: To watch energy pass through a row of still steel balls, as it did through your line of coins.
videos.check: Id confirmed with YouTube (title and channel match). Length is an estimate. A parent should preview it first.

videos.title: Demonstration of Conservation of Energy by Professor Walter Lewin
videos.why: For the parent and child together: a physicist lets a heavy pendulum swing back towards his own chin, trusting that it can never return higher than it started.
videos.check: Id confirmed with YouTube (title and channel match). It is a re-upload of a lecture clip from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Length is an estimate. A parent should preview it first.

quiz.p: A hot dosa is put on a cold steel plate. The plate warms up. What is this?
quiz.why: Heat passes from the dosa to the plate, and it is heat before and after. That is a transfer. If you chose a change of form, look for a new form. There is none here.

quiz.p: You ring a cycle bell with your thumb. Which change of form happens?
quiz.why: Your thumb moves the lever, the bell shakes, and the shaking air is sound. If you chose another, say each form aloud and check that it is really there.

quiz.p: Which energy chain fits a torch?
quiz.why: The cell holds stored chemical energy. It becomes electrical energy in the wires and then light and a little warmth in the bulb. The second chain runs backwards, which is what a solar panel does.

quiz.p: A marble rolls down a slope. What happens to its energy on the way down?
opts: Stored energy changes into movement energy
Movement energy changes into stored energy
New energy is made by rolling
quiz.why: It loses height and gains speed, so stored energy is changing into movement energy. Rolling makes no new energy. The energy was put in when the marble was lifted.

quiz.p: A ball rolls across the floor and stops. Where is its movement energy now?
opts: Warmth in the floor, ball and air
Back inside the ball as movement
quiz.why: Friction changed the movement into warmth, spread through the floor, the ball and the air. 'Gone' is how it looks, but each time it is measured the warmth matches the lost movement.

quiz.p: A flat torch cell shows that energy can be used up and destroyed.
quiz.why: False. The energy that was stored in the cell is now warmth spread through the room. What ran out was energy gathered in one place.

quiz.p: A marble starts 5 centimetres high and pushes a cup 4 centimetres. From 10 centimetres high, about how far will it push?
quiz.why: Twice the height stores twice the energy, and that pushes the cup about twice as far: about 8 centimetres. If you chose 4, you expected height not to matter. Try the test again and compare.

quiz.p: In the marble and cup test, why is each start mark tried three times?
quiz.why: A single roll can be odd. Three rolls let you take the middle value, which a single odd roll cannot spoil. The marble and the cup do not change.

quiz.p: For a ceiling fan, which is the useful energy?
quiz.why: A fan is built to move air. The warm motor and the hum are energy that spread out where we did not want it.

quiz.p: On a cold night in Ooty, a family is glad of the warmth from an old bulb. Is that warmth wasted?
quiz.why: Useful means 'what we wanted'. Tonight the warmth is wanted, so it is useful. Energy is never destroyed, and no form of energy is waste by its nature.

quiz.p: In which of these is work done on the thing, in the scientist's meaning?
opts: Lifting a bucket from a well
Pushing a wall that stays put
quiz.why: Work needs a force and a movement. The bucket moves up, so energy passes to it. The bag and the wall do not move, so no energy passes to them, though your muscles still spend energy.

quiz.p: Which is the best description of what physicists mean by energy?
opts: A number whose total never changes
quiz.why: Energy is a number that can be worked out for anything, and its total stays the same through every change. Nobody has found a liquid, and what energy is underneath is still unknown.

quiz.p: Scientists know exactly what energy is made of.
quiz.why: False. They can work out the amount exactly, and it always balances. What energy is, underneath the sums, is an open question.

worksheets.title: Pass it on or change it (core)

items.p: A cricket bat hits a ball and the ball flies off. What is this mainly?
opts: A change of sound into light
items.why: Movement energy passes from the bat to the ball. The form stays the same, so it is a transfer.

items.p: In an energy change, the energy turns into a different form.
items.why: True. A clap changes movement into sound. A bulb changes electrical energy into light.

items.p: When energy passes from one thing to another, it is called an energy ____.
items.why: A transfer is energy passing along. A change, or transformation, is energy taking a new form.

items.p: Sort each event by what the energy mainly does.
items: a striker hits a carrom coin
Passes along (transfer)
warm hands warm a cold cheek
Passes along (transfer)
one swing bumps the next swing
Passes along (transfer)
a clap makes a sound
Changes form
a torch cell lights a bulb
Changes form
a marble speeds up down a slope
Changes form
rubbed palms get warm
Changes form
items.a: as given
items.why: In the first three, the energy is the same form before and after, and only moves to a new thing. In the last four, a new form appears.

items.p: Match each thing to the main energy change it makes.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Ask what goes in and what comes out. A solar panel runs a torch's chain backwards.

items.p: Put the steps of a torch's energy chain in order.
a: Stored chemical energy in the cell
Light and warmth from the bulb
A slightly warmer wall and room
items.why: The energy starts in the cell, is carried round the loop, becomes light and warmth in the bulb, and ends as warmth in the room.

items.p: A paper cup slides and stops. What changed its movement energy into warmth?
items.why: Friction between the cup and the table changes movement into warmth. Gravity pulls down, and does not slow a cup sliding on a level table.

items.p: Pushing hard on a wall that does not move does work on the wall.
items.why: False. In science, work is a force moving a thing. The wall does not move, so no energy passes to it.

items.p: The part of the energy that does the job we wanted is called ____ energy.
items.why: For a bulb the useful energy is light. For a fan it is moving air.

items.p: Draw an energy chain for a ceiling fan, from the wall switch to the room. Use boxes and arrows.
items.a: Boxes such as: electrical energy in the wires → motor → moving blades → moving air → warmth in the room. A side arrow from the motor shows warmth and hum.
items.why: A good chain has an arrow for every step, shows the useful part, and follows the energy until it has spread out as warmth.

items.p: A football rolls across a field and stops. A friend says its energy is gone. What would you say to her?
items.a: The energy is not gone. Friction with the grass and the air changed the ball's movement into warmth. The grass, the ball and the air are each a tiny bit warmer.
items.why: A strong answer says where the energy went and that the amount is the same as before.

items.p: A mixer grinder makes chutney. Which is spread-out energy?
opts: The roar and the warm jar
items.why: The mixer is built to turn its blades and cut. The noise and warmth are energy that went where it was not wanted.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? A kettle, an iron, a geyser, a fan.
items.a: The fan, because it changes electrical energy mainly into movement. The other three change it mainly into heat.
items.why: Look at the main form that comes out. Three give heat and one gives movement.

items.p: Two children look at a toy car that has rolled to a stop.

views.says: The car used up its energy. That is why it stopped.
The car's energy is still here. It is in the floor and the air as warmth.

items.ask: Which child do you agree with more? What could you do to check?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer says the second child matches what measurements find, and that the first child is right that the car's own movement energy ran down. A check is to rub something hard and feel the warmth.
items.why: The first child describes what we see: the gathered movement energy has run down. The second describes what is measured: the same amount now exists as warmth.

items.p: A marble pushed a cup 3, 5 and 4 centimetres in three tries. What is the middle value?
items.why: In order the tries are 3, 4, 5. The middle one is 4 centimetres.

items.p: Name one thing in your home that changes energy from one form to another. Say what goes in and what comes out.
items.a: Any true example, such as: a television takes in electrical energy and gives out light, sound and warmth.
items.why: A strong answer names the form going in, the useful form coming out, and at least one spread-out form.

items.p: A wave crosses a pond and a floating leaf only bobs up and down. What travelled across the pond?
items.why: The water and the leaf stayed in their places and only moved up and down. The energy of the wave travelled across.

items.p: Sound can carry energy through the air without the air travelling to your ear.
items.why: True. Each bit of air shakes and pushes the next bit. The shaking travels, and the air stays roughly where it was.

items.p: A drawing where the width of each arrow shows the share of energy is called an energy ____ diagram.
items.why: The arrow in is as wide as all the arrows out added together, because no energy is made or lost.

items.p: A girl throws a ball straight up and catches it. Put the energy forms in order from the throw.
a: Stored energy in her arm muscles
Movement energy of the rising ball
Stored energy of height at the top
Movement energy of the falling ball
Warmth and sound in her hands at the catch
items.why: Her muscles give the ball movement. Going up, movement changes into stored energy of height. Coming down it changes back, and the catch turns it into warmth and a slap of sound.

items.p: Match each living being to an energy change it makes.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Every living being takes energy in one form and changes it to others. A leaf and a firefly run opposite changes.

items.p: A bulb's arrow in is 10 squares wide. Its light arrow is 3 squares wide. How wide is the warmth arrow?
items.why: The arrows out must add up to the arrow in. 10 take away 3 is 7 squares.

items.p: A swing is at the very top of its swing, about to come back. Where is most of its energy?
items.why: At the top it is highest and, for a moment, still. So the energy is stored in height. At the bottom of the swing it is nearly all movement.

items.p: A pendulum let go from a mark can swing back higher than that mark by itself.
items.why: False. It can never have more energy than it started with, and it loses a little to the air on each swing. So it returns a little lower each time.

items.p: In the Tired Swing test, an open card made the keys stop swinging much sooner. Explain why, using the word energy.
items.a: The open card pushes much more air aside on every swing. Pushing air changes the swing's movement energy into warmth in the air, so the energy leaves the swing sooner.
items.why: A strong answer says where the energy went (the air) and why more went there with the open card (more air to push).

items.p: Sort each one by how the energy is mainly transferred.
items: lifting a bucket on a rope
By a push or pull (work)
a bat hitting a ball
By a push or pull (work)
a hot tawa cooking a dosa
By heating
warm hands melting a piece of ice
By heating
sunshine drying clothes on a line
By sound or light
a temple bell heard across a street
By sound or light
items.a: as given
items.why: A force that moves a thing transfers energy as work. A hotter thing touching a cooler one transfers it by heating. Sound and light carry it across a gap as waves.

items.p: Lifting a bottle of water 1 metre takes about 10 joules. About how many joules to lift it 3 metres?
items.why: Three times the distance is three times the work. 10 times 3 is 30 joules.

items.p: Draw an energy flow diagram for an old bulb with a glowing wire. Make the arrows the right widths.
items.a: One wide arrow in, labelled electrical. It splits into a very thin arrow labelled light and a very wide arrow labelled heat.
items.why: Only about a twentieth becomes light, so the light arrow is thin and the heat arrow takes nearly all the width.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Holding a bag still, lifting a bag, pulling a cart, kicking a ball.
items.a: Holding a bag still, because nothing moves, so no work is done on the bag. In the other three, a force moves a thing.
items.why: Work in science needs movement. Three of these have it and one does not.

items.p: Is the warmth from your body wasted energy?

views.says: Yes. Your muscles turn only a quarter of the food energy into movement. The rest is lost as heat.
No. That warmth keeps your body at the temperature it needs. Without it you would not live.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with more? Can both be true?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer sees that 'wasted' depends on the job you have in mind. For moving, the warmth is a loss. For staying alive, it is needed.
items.why: Both use the same facts. The engineer counts only movement as the job. The biologist counts staying warm as a job too. Useful is about what is wanted.

items.p: Explain why a bouncing ball bounces a little lower each time.
items.a: At each bounce the ball is squashed and springs back. Some of its movement energy changes into warmth in the rubber and the floor, and into sound. So it has less energy to rise with.
items.why: A strong answer names where the energy goes at each bounce, and says the energy is not destroyed.

items.p: You want to find out if a rough table stops the cup sooner than a smooth one. What must you change?
opts: The start mark and the cup
items.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. Here it is the surface. If the marble or the start mark changed too, you could not tell what made the difference.

items.p: Julius Robert Mayer said in 1842 that movement and heat are the same thing in two forms. Which finding fits his idea?
opts: A heavy wheel turns for ever
items.why: If movement and heat are one, then lost movement must show up as warmth, and it does. No wheel has ever turned for ever.

items.p: An energy chain for a bus could begin with sunlight that fell millions of years ago.
items.why: True. Diesel is made from tiny sea beings that lived long ago and stored the energy of sunlight. That stored energy is what moves the bus.

items.p: The rule that energy is never made and never destroyed is called the ____ of energy.
items.why: Conservation means the total is kept. Energy only moves and changes form.

items.p: Put this energy chain in order, starting from the earliest.
a: Water rises as vapour and falls as rain in the hills
Water rushes down through a turbine at a dam
A fan turns in a flat
items.why: The Sun lifts the water. The high water stores energy. Falling, it turns a turbine and a generator, and the electrical energy runs the fan.

items.p: A machine takes in 100 joules. It gives 25 joules of movement. How many joules spread out as warmth and sound?
items.why: Nothing is lost, so the rest must be warmth and sound. 100 take away 25 is 75 joules.

items.p: Bhaskara II described a wheel meant to turn for ever. Why does every such wheel stop?
opts: Friction changes its movement into warmth
items.why: On every turn a little movement becomes warmth at the axle and in the air. Nothing puts that energy back, so the wheel slows and stops.

items.p: In 1930 some atoms seemed to lose energy. Wolfgang Pauli guessed an unseen particle took it. Why was that bold?
items.a: Nobody had seen such a particle. He trusted the rule that energy is never lost more than he trusted that everything had been seen. The particle, the neutrino, was found in 1956.
items.why: A strong answer says that he had two choices: give up the rule, or predict something new. He kept the rule, and a test later agreed.

items.p: People who study energy use different words for what you saw today.

views.says: Energy has forms, and it changes from one form to another.

views.who: The Institute of Physics in Britain
views.says: Energy does not change form. It is shifted from one store to another along a pathway.
Energy is a number we work out. Both sets of words are ways of keeping the accounts.

items.ask: Which way of speaking helps you most to think about a torch? Say why.
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer tries one of the ways on the torch and says what it makes clear and what it hides.
items.why: No view is marked right here, because teachers and physicists still disagree. All three give the same amounts. They differ in the picture they put in your mind.

items.p: Draw what happens to the atoms of a table top just under a sliding cup. Show before and after.
items.a: Before: rows of atoms jiggling a little. After: the same atoms jiggling more, in all directions, under where the cup slid.
items.why: Warmth is the scattered movement of atoms. Friction turns the one orderly movement of the cup into faster jiggling of many atoms.

items.p: Emmy Noether proved why energy is conserved. What is the reason she found?
opts: The laws of nature stay the same over time
Energy is too heavy to vanish
items.why: She showed in 1918 that if the laws of nature are the same from one moment to the next, a number must stay constant. That number is energy.

items.p: If a marble starts twice as high on a slope, it reaches the bottom twice as fast.
items.why: False. It arrives with twice the movement energy, but movement energy grows faster than speed. Its speed is only about one and a half times as great.

items.p: Design a fair test: does a heavier marble push the cup further? Say what changes and what stays the same.
items.a: Change only the marble: a small one and a big one. Keep the ramp, the start mark, the cup and the table the same. Roll each three times and compare the middle slides.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing, keeps the rest the same, repeats each roll, and says what will be measured.

items.p: Match each person to what they did.
pairs: showed that rubbing makes heat without end
measured how much movement makes how much heat
proved why energy must be conserved
showed that a wire's energy travels in the space around it
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each one added a piece. Rumford and Joule joined movement to heat. Poynting followed the energy of a circuit. Noether found the reason for the rule.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Warm brakes, a warm phone charger, a warm motor, a warm cup of tea.
items.a: The warm cup of tea, because its warmth is the useful energy we wanted. In the other three, the warmth is spread-out energy we did not want.
items.why: Useful depends on the job. Tea is meant to be hot. Brakes, chargers and motors are not built to make warmth.

items.p: The total energy in the world never changes. So why do people say we must save energy?
items.a: What we can run short of is gathered energy in a useful form, such as fuel, food and charged batteries. Once it has spread out as warmth it is very hard to use again. Saving energy means spreading it out more slowly.
items.why: A strong answer separates the amount of energy, which is fixed, from how gathered and useful it is, which runs down.

items.p: You push a toy car 2 metres. Then you push it just as hard for 4 metres. Which push did more work?
items.why: Work depends on the force and on how far the thing moves. The same force over twice the distance does twice the work.

applications: Hydroelectric stations such as Idukki in Kerala change the stored energy of high water into movement and then into electrical energy.
Wind farms such as Muppandal in Tamil Nadu transfer the movement energy of air to turning blades.
Solar parks such as Pavagada in Karnataka and Bhadla in Rajasthan change light straight into electrical energy.
Electric trains and some electric cars use their motors as generators when braking, to change movement back into stored electrical energy.
Engineers draw energy flow diagrams to find where a factory, a car or a house lets energy spread out, and to cut the loss.
LED bulbs give the same light as older bulbs for a fraction of the electricity, because less becomes heat.
Pressure cookers and pots with lids keep heat from spreading into the kitchen, so more of it cooks the food.
Musicians and makers of instruments such as the ghatam and the veena shape wood and clay so that hand movement changes well into sound.

open_questions.q: What is energy, underneath the sums?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists can work out the number exactly and it always balances. Nobody can say what it is a number of, or if that question even has an answer.

open_questions.q: Is the total energy of the whole universe fixed, zero, changing, or impossible to add up?
open_questions.why_open: Einstein's theory of gravity gives no single way to count the energy of stretching space, so careful physicists reach different answers.

open_questions.q: Why does energy spread out but never gather itself back?
open_questions.why_open: The rule of conservation would allow both. The spreading seems to depend on the universe having started in a very special, gathered state, and nobody knows why it started that way.

open_questions.q: What is the dark energy that makes space stretch faster and faster?
open_questions.why_open: It was found in 1998 by measuring far exploding stars. It seems to be most of the energy in the universe, and nobody knows what it is.

open_questions.q: How do leaves pass the energy of light from molecule to molecule with almost none lost on the way?
open_questions.why_open: In 2007 a team reported that leaves may use quantum effects to do it. Later tests questioned this, and the work goes on.

maths.problem: In the Marble and the Cup test, three rolls from the top mark pushed the cup 12, 15 and 13 centimetres. What is the middle value?
maths.explain: Put the three in order: 12, 13, 15. The middle one is 13.
maths.context: In the Marble and the Cup test, you roll a marble into a cup three times from each height.
maths.why_maths: A middle value gives one fair number for three tries, so that one odd roll does not mislead you.

maths.problem: From a height of 3 centimetres a marble pushed a cup 4 centimetres. If the push grows in step with the height, how far would it push from 9 centimetres?
maths.explain: 9 is 3 times 3, so the push is 3 times 4, which is 12 centimetres.
maths.context: In the Marble and the Cup test, you check whether the push grows in step with the starting height.
maths.why_maths: If two things grow in step, you can predict one from the other and then test your prediction.

maths.problem: A kettle takes 100 joules of electrical energy. Four fifths of it heats the water. How many joules heat the water, and how many spread out?
maths.answer: 80 joules heat the water and 20 joules spread out.
maths.explain: One fifth of 100 is 20. Four fifths is 80. 100 take away 80 leaves 20.
maths.context: An electric kettle changes electrical energy into heat, and most of that heat goes into the water.
maths.why_maths: A fraction tells you the share of the energy that did the job, which is how machines are compared.

maths.problem: Three players start the Warmth Bowl game with 12 beans each, and the Sun pile has 10. At the end the players hold 9, 7 and 11 beans and the Sun pile has 2. How many beans are in the bowl?
maths.explain: At the start there are 36 and 10, which is 46. At the end the hands hold 27 and the Sun has 2, which is 29. 46 take away 29 is 17.
maths.context: In the Warmth Bowl game, beans stand for energy and the total number of beans never changes.
maths.why_maths: Because the total never changes, you can find a missing amount by subtracting, which is how scientists find where energy went.

maths.problem: In the Tired Swing test, the keys made 48 swings with the card folded and 6 swings with it open. How many times sooner did the open card run down?
maths.context: In the Tired Swing test, you count how many swings a pendulum makes before it is half as wide.
maths.why_maths: Dividing tells you how many times bigger one result is than another, which is a clearer comparison than the difference.

maths.problem: An old bulb takes in 60 joules each second and gives 3 joules of light. An LED bulb takes in 9 joules each second and gives 3 joules of light. How many joules become warmth in each bulb every second?
maths.answer: 57 joules in the old bulb and 6 joules in the LED bulb.
maths.explain: 60 take away 3 is 57. 9 take away 3 is 6. Both give the same light, but the old bulb spreads out far more warmth.
maths.context: A bulb changes electrical energy into light and warmth, and different bulbs share it out differently.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting the useful part from the total shows how much energy spread out, so you can compare two machines.

maths.problem: Draw a bar chart for cup slides of 4, 9 and 13 centimetres from the three marks. Use one square for each centimetre. How many squares taller is the tallest bar than the shortest?
maths.explain: The tallest bar is 13 squares and the shortest is 4. 13 take away 4 is 9.
maths.context: In the Marble and the Cup test, you draw the three middle slides as bars.
maths.why_maths: Bars let you see at a glance whether the push grows in step with the height.

roots.context: You have watched a marble pass its energy to a cup, and the cup pass it to the table. Now we ask what that tells us about the things of the world, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In the Marble and the Cup test, the marble stopped and the cup slid. Then the cup stopped, and the table grew a tiny bit warmer. The energy did not stay with any of them. Each one held it for a moment and passed it on. So a marble, a cup or a body is a place that energy is passing through.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'the marble's energy' and 'my energy', as if each thing owned a share and kept it. That way of speaking splits the world into owners and their belongings. The test shows that nothing keeps what it is given.
deep_truth.evidence: The cup slid further when the marble started higher, though nobody touched the cup. The height came from your arm, your arm's energy from breakfast, and breakfast from the Sun. After the cup stopped, the same amount had moved on into the table and the air.

three.who_am_i: The energy that lifts your arm was sunlight a few months ago, and it will be warmth in the air a few minutes from now. You are one of the places where it is passing through, and you are awake while it passes.
three.what_is_life: A living body is a chain of energy changes that never stops. Food comes in, and movement, warmth, thought and voice go out. When the passing stops, the body stops.
three.what_is_this_world: From the Sun to a leaf to a parrot to the warm air, one amount is handed along and never grows or shrinks. The things we name are the stations on its way.

roots.thread: Follow any chain in this lesson and you never find a place where the energy begins, and you never find a place where it ends. You only find where it was before, and where it went next. The torch, the kettle, the marble, the potter's wheel and your own hand are all joined by one handing-on that has no gap in it. Science counts the amount and finds it always the same. That one amount, showing up as light in one place and warmth in another, is a clear picture of the One appearing as many. Consciousness is the ground from which all of it arises, and the energy in a marble and the energy in the hand that lifts it are one movement of that ground. Many scientists do not accept this last step, and their view is given below.

teachings.teaching: The sage Uddalaka tells his son Shvetaketu that by knowing one lump of clay, everything made of clay is known. The pot and the plate are different names that speech gives. What is real in all of them is the clay.
teachings.link: Light, sound, movement and warmth are names for what energy is doing. In every one of them the amount is the same energy, as every pot is the same clay.

teachings.teaching: Laozi says that the Way gives rise to one, one gives rise to two, two gives rise to three, and three gives rise to the ten thousand things.
teachings.link: One store of sunlight becomes rice, then a push, then a spinning wheel, a sound and a warm hand. One energy becomes many happenings.

teachings.teaching: Krishna tells Arjuna that as a person takes off worn clothes and puts on new ones, so the one who lives in the body leaves worn bodies and enters new ones.
teachings.link: The Gita speaks of the self. Energy offers a picture of the same shape: it leaves one form and takes another, and is itself never worn out.

science.text: In every event ever measured, the total energy before equals the total energy after.
Emmy Noether proved in 1918 that energy is conserved because the laws of nature do not change from one moment to the next.
Energy may be a real thing that flows, or only a number in our accounts. Physicists hold both views.
What energy is, underneath the sums, is not known. Whether it has anything to do with consciousness is not a question physics can test today.

other_view.who: The Buddha, in the Anattalakkhana Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 22.59), and many physicists today
other_view.view: The Buddha taught that there is change after change with no lasting self or substance underneath. On this view there is no one clay that takes many shapes. There is only the passing-on. Many physicists say something close to this about energy: it is a number that balances, and not a thing or a ground. They add that nothing in the measurements points to consciousness.

practice.title: The hand-on
practice.say: Sit facing each other. Rub your palms together fast, ten times. Now press your warm palms gently against the other person's palms and close your eyes. Feel the warmth pass across. Breathe slowly three times. Ask yourself quietly: where was this warmth this morning? Where will it be tonight?
practice.kid: Rub your palms ten times. Press them on a grown-up's palms. Feel the warmth pass. Breathe slowly three times. Where will the warmth go next?

ask: If nothing keeps the energy it is given, in what way is the energy in your body yours?
Is energy one thing wearing many forms, or only many changes with nothing underneath? How could anyone tell?
The amount of energy never changes, but its form always does. Is there anything about you that is like that?
