playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. The Marble and the Cup was worked out on paper. A 5 gram marble rolling off a 10 centimetre rise reaches about 1 metre a second. It should push a 5 gram paper cup about 10 to 18 centimetres on a smooth table, and about a third of that from the lowest mark. Real cups and tables differ, so the steps say to write what you see, and give fixes for a cup that tips or hardly moves. The Tired Swing counts are estimates: tens of swings with the card folded and fewer than ten with it open. The Coin Line works best with smooth coins of one kind, and two coins in together is harder to do cleanly. The plain card top in the Long Spin spins for only a few seconds, which the steps say. Facts to check before this goes live: a kettle putting about four fifths of its energy into the water; an old bulb giving about a twentieth as light and an LED about a third; a squash ball reaching about 45 degrees Celsius; Rumford's two and a half hours; the dates 1150, 1775, 1798, 1829, 1842, 1847, 1884, 1918, 1924, 1925, 1930 and 1956; the wording of Chandogya Upanishad 6.1.4, Tao Te Ching 42 and Bhagavad Gita 2.22. how_we_found_out.story: About 1150, the Indian astronomer Bhaskara II described a wheel with curved spokes half filled with mercury. He reasoned that one side would always be heavier, so the wheel would turn for ever. It was a sensible idea, because a heavy side does fall. For the next six hundred years, inventors in the Arab world and in Europe drew and built such wheels. Every one slowed and stopped. In 1775 the Royal Academy of Sciences in Paris refused to examine any more of them. Nobody could yet say why they failed. In 1798 Count Rumford showed that rubbing makes heat without end. In 1842 a German ship's doctor, Julius Robert Mayer, wrote that movement and heat are one thing in two forms. In the 1840s James Joule measured it. In 1847 Hermann von Helmholtz put it all together. Energy is never made or lost, so a wheel that loses a little to friction on each turn must stop.
how_we_found_out.who: Bhaskara II, Count Rumford, Julius Robert Mayer, James Joule and Hermann von Helmholtz
how_we_found_out.when: About 1150 for the wheel, and 1775 to 1847 for the answer
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: For centuries many clever people thought that a well-made wheel could keep itself turning for ever. Every wheel that was built stopped, and by 1847 scientists could say why: friction turns a little movement into warmth on every turn, and nothing puts it back.
how_we_found_out.context: Can a machine keep itself going for ever? This card tells the true story of a wheel first described in India, and how its failure led to the rule that energy is never made or lost.

quiz: When a coin hits a still coin and it moves off, energy has been transferred.
Movement energy passed from the first coin to the second.
A clap changes movement energy into sound.
The moving hands stop, and the air is set shaking.
A ball that stops has destroyed its energy.
The energy has become warmth in the ball, the ground and the air.
A torch changes stored energy into electrical energy and then into light.
The cell's chemicals hold the store, and the bulb makes the light.
A marble at the top of a slope has more movement energy than at the bottom.
At the top its energy is stored in height. At the bottom it is movement.
Holding a bag perfectly still does work on the bag.
Work needs a force and a movement. The bag does not move.
Friction changes movement into warmth.
Rub your palms together and you can feel it.
An LED bulb spreads out less warmth than an old bulb for the same light.
More of its electrical energy becomes light.
Sound carries energy without the air travelling from the drum to your ear.
The shaking is passed along. The air stays roughly in its place.
Physicists know exactly what energy is made of.
They can work out the amount exactly, but what it is underneath is unknown.
odd: A fan gives mainly movement. The other three give mainly heat.
A clap changes movement into sound. The other three pass movement to another thing.
Nothing moves, so no work is done on the bag.
The light is the useful energy. The other three are spread-out energy.
A firefly gives out light. The other three take light in.
